A voice agent needs four things working together in under a second: speech recognition to hear the caller, a language model to decide what happens next, speech synthesis to reply, and telephony to carry the call. Orchestration coordinates them. It decides when the caller has finished speaking, stops the agent mid-word when someone interrupts, holds conversation state across turns, and calls your systems while the caller waits.
### Orchestration frameworks: build the pipeline yourself
These are libraries rather than products. They handle the hard parts of real-time voice and leave you the rest, including hosting, model contracts, observability and upgrades.
Either way you buy components separately. Teams commonly use Deepgram and Sarvam AI for speech recognition, ElevenLabs and Cartesia for speech synthesis, and OpenAI's Realtime API for speech-to-speech.
#### LiveKit
LiveKit is an open-source realtime framework under Apache 2.0, with an agents SDK built for voice. You write agent logic in Python or Node.js, choose your own speech and language models, and get turn detection and interruption handling from the framework. Telephony comes from LiveKit SIP, a first-party service that sits alongside the agents SDK rather than inside it, and that you deploy separately if you self-host.
You can run agents on LiveKit Cloud or in your own environment, and that second path matters for teams whose residency rules block managed infrastructure.
Best for:
engineering teams that need control over the media layer and expect to keep customising after launch.
#### Pipecat
Pipecat is an open-source Python framework, BSD-2 licensed and maintained by Daily, that treats a voice agent as a pipeline of processors handling audio, text and video in real time. You can swap speech, language and vision services across a large provider catalogue, usually in one line of code, so each model earns its place on cost and accuracy rather than arriving in a bundle. The framework manages conversation context across turns, and its smart turn detection decides when a caller has finished rather than relying on voice activity detection alone.
Provider neutrality is the point of the design, which helps when you expect model providers to change underneath you, or when you want to benchmark options inside the framework you will run in production.
Python teams that want full control over model selection without committing to a hosted platform.
### Managed orchestration platforms: configure the pipeline
These platforms own the orchestration layer and let you supply the models. You give up control of the runtime and get back the months of engineering that turn detection, interruption handling and state management would otherwise cost.
#### Vapi
Vapi gives you a dashboard for building and editing assistants alongside full REST API access, so operations and engineering can work on the same agent from different directions. You bring your own provider keys for transcription, language and voice, choosing each one independently, and telephony arrives with the platform, including custom SIP, warm transfers and DTMF. Vapi retired its visual Workflows builder in August 2026, so judge it on the current dashboard and Squads rather than on older documentation.
Deployment runs in the cloud by default. Vapi offers on-premise to large enterprise customers on negotiated terms, and lists data residency on its enterprise tier alongside SOC 2, HIPAA and PCI.
teams that want to move quickly across web, phone and in-app channels while keeping code-level control of the agent.
#### Retell
Retell puts most of its engineering into conversational quality. A proprietary turn-taking model targets the pause between a caller finishing and the agent replying, and you can tune interruption sensitivity so the agent holds up in noisy environments. Retell publishes an average end-to-end latency of about 600 milliseconds, measured by the vendor rather than audited. You can buy Retell-managed numbers or connect your own carrier over SIP trunking, and a JavaScript SDK handles browser calls.
Its managed cloud currently runs from one AWS region with more planned, and Retell offers on-premise deployment for organisations with stricter residency rules.
consumer-facing voice agents where naturalness and response latency decide whether callers stay on the line.
### Full-stack voice AI agent platforms: deploy an agent
These vendors own more of the stack, which cuts integration work and narrows how much of the conversation design you control. Where security review, language coverage and time to production dominate the decision, that trade usually favours the platform.
One distinction deserves care. Several platforms here offer on-premise deployment, so the question is not whether a vendor supports it but what actually runs locally. In many cases the orchestration and application layer deploy into your environment while model inference still depends on a third party, which leaves the residency question open even though the software sits on your servers.
#### Gnani AI
Gnani AI builds voice agents on models it develops in-house. Prisma v2.5 handles speech recognition, trained on 14 million hours of proprietary Indic speech across 12 languages, with native GSM and VoIP codec handling and word-level code-switching that needs no language tag. Timbre v2.5 handles synthesis, a streaming neural TTS with context-aware prosody. Reasoning runs on the Evon family, with Evon v2.0 covering enterprise reasoning across 11 Indic languages for banking, insurance, healthcare and telecom. Speech recognition reaches further than reasoning does, covering 40 or more languages including 12 or more Indic ones, which is a distinction worth holding onto when you compare language counts across vendors. Gnani Agents is the layer enterprises deploy on top, covering inbound and outbound voice with tool calling, human handoff and auditable records of each interaction.
Published speech recognition results.
Gnani AI benchmarks Prisma v2.5 against ElevenLabs Scribe v2, Deepgram Nova-3, Sarvam Saaras v3 and Microsoft Azure STT on public evaluation datasets, scoring every provider through its production API with no audio enhancement or pre-processing and computing metrics with the jiwer library. On GramVaani, the rural Hindi set that best represents how Tier 2 and Tier 3 callers actually speak, Prisma v2.5 records 22.0% word error rate against Sarvam at 23.4%, Microsoft at 26.4%, ElevenLabs at 27.5% and Deepgram at 34.0%. On Kathbath, word error rate runs from 7.6% in Hindi through 13.9% in Marathi to 20.4% in Tamil and 27.7% in Malayalam. Across 48 evaluations Prisma v2.5 ranks first in 27, and leads in 8 of the 9 languages tested.
One result runs the other way and is worth knowing before you build a business case on it. Moving from clean to noisy audio, Prisma v2.5 degrades by 3.6 percentage points where Sarvam Saaras v3 degrades by 2.6, though both hold up considerably better than Microsoft at 7.8 and ElevenLabs at 12.2. Gnani AI also recommends character error rate rather than word error rate for Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam, since word-level scoring penalises agglutinative languages in ways that overstate real transcription failure.
Gnani AI does not currently publish entity-level accuracy, which is the measure this article recommends you weight most heavily for BFSI work. Ask for it on your own audio, as you should of any vendor on this list.
At the agent level, Gnani AI publishes response latency under 800 milliseconds in live conversations and runs more than 30 million conversations a day across deployments, which is a useful proxy for whether concurrency holds at scale.
Owning the pipeline end to end changes how you tune latency, because recognition, reasoning and synthesis get optimised together rather than negotiated across three vendor contracts.
Gnani Artha takes this further, bringing the models, the agent platform and the infrastructure inside the enterprise perimeter, running on-premise or in a VPC on a single node. Evon v3.3 is a 30-billion-parameter open-weights model with 3.5 billion active parameters covering 11 Indian languages, published under Apache 2.0 on Hugging Face and built with a tokenizer designed for Indic scripts. Because the weights run locally, your deployment architecture answers DPDP, RBI and IRDAI residency questions instead of a contract clause about someone else's model.
regulated enterprises running multilingual voice agents at scale, where the model weights need to sit inside your own environment and callers move between Indian languages during a call.
ENTERPRISE VOICE AI
See Gnani AI's Voice AI Agent in action
200+ Enterprises · 30M daily calls · 10 Indic languages
Book A Demo
#### Kore.ai
Kore.ai is an enterprise agentic AI platform, repositioned from conversational AI with its Artemis release in May 2026, covering voice and digital channels on shared infrastructure. It supports no-code and pro-code authoring, pairing a visual workspace with a purpose-built agent definition language, and publishes a large connector catalogue reaching enterprise systems and core banking. Kore.ai enforces governance at the platform layer rather than inside the model, logging every agent action so you can trace it to a specific control.
It offers the broadest deployment range here, covering public cloud, sovereign regions, private cloud and on-premise with regional data residency. That breadth is the reason to evaluate it and the reason evaluations take time, since programmes usually involve configuration and integration work rather than a fast pilot.
large enterprises standardising many interaction types on one governed platform under central IT.
#### Uniphore
Uniphore now sells itself as a horizontal enterprise AI company rather than a CX specialist. Its Business AI Cloud spans data, knowledge, models and agents across marketing, sales, HR and IT as well as customer service. Voice agents and conversation analytics share one platform, so consolidating cuts the number of parties touching call audio and shortens security review. A zero-copy architecture keeps data where it already sits, and deployment covers cloud, multi-cloud and on-premise.
That breadth means your evaluation should pin down which capabilities are in scope and how Uniphore licenses them, since the platform reaches well past contact centre work.
enterprises consolidating agents and conversation analytics across several business functions rather than in the contact centre alone.
#### Observe.AI
Observe.AI grew out of conversation intelligence and agent assist, and has extended into autonomous voice agents on the same platform, handling inbound and outbound service work end to end across voice and chat. That history shows in the quality management and analytics tooling, which earns its keep when the programme covers improving human agent performance alongside automating calls.
Deployment is where Observe.AI narrows your options. It hosts only on AWS, with no on-premise or customer-VPC path, offering per-customer storage with unique encryption keys instead. Where your security review accepts a well-controlled SaaS arrangement that works cleanly, and where you need processing inside your own perimeter it rules the platform out early.
contact centres running call automation and agent performance management together, where SaaS deployment is acceptable.
#### Skit.ai
Skit.ai is a US-based company focused on collections and recovery for lenders, banks and agencies, with agents that reach consumers across voice, SMS, email and chat. It supports inbound and outbound flows, and offers multilingual conversations with Hindi and English coverage in its India operations. The narrow scope shapes conversation design, compliance handling and reporting around the collections workflow rather than exposing a general-purpose builder.
That depth helps when the use case matches and constrains you when the roadmap moves into general servicing or other verticals.
collections and recovery operations that want a purpose-built system rather than a general platform.
### How to evaluate an AI voice agent platform
#### Latency: what to measure and what to target
Measure end-to-end response time from the moment the caller stops speaking to the moment audio starts playing back, rather than component latency on its own. For calibration, research on human conversation finds gaps between turns of about 200 milliseconds, and work on spoken dialogue systems suggests delays past roughly 700 milliseconds read as hesitation while pauses past two seconds read as a breakdown. Vendors publish their own latency figures without independent audit, so treat them as claims to test.
Insist on measurement under your own conditions, because telephony adds round-trip time a browser demo never shows.
Ask the vendor:
what is your p95 end-to-end response latency on a PSTN call in our primary market, how did you measure it, and can we reproduce it on our own trunk?
#### Accuracy on your vocabulary, not benchmark audio
Word error rate on clean benchmark audio says little about performance on your calls, and the gap between clean and telephony conditions is where models separate. Entity accuracy decides outcomes: account numbers, policy numbers, names, amounts and dates. You cannot recover an error at that level downstream, because every step after it reasons confidently from a wrong value.
When a vendor shows you benchmark results, check which datasets they used and whether the audio matched your conditions. A model tested on studio recordings will behave differently on an 8kHz mobile call from a Tier 3 town. Ask which scoring library computed the numbers and whether any pre-processing touched the audio first.
can we run our own call audio through your recognition model before signing, and will you report entity-level accuracy separately from word error rate?
#### Language coverage and code-switching
Language counts tell you less than they appear to, and vendors count different things. Speech recognition coverage is usually wider than the set a reasoning model can actually operate in, so a platform advertising 40 languages may reason in a third of them. What matters beyond the count is whether the system handles a caller switching languages inside one sentence, whether accuracy holds across regional accents, and whether synthesis sounds natural beyond English.
how many languages does your recognition model cover, how many can the reasoning model work in, and can you show mid-sentence switching on our audio?
#### Telephony and contact centre integration
Most enterprises already run telephony and a contact centre platform, which makes integration more relevant than a platform's native calling features. Establish where the SIP leg terminates, how the agent hands off to a human with context intact, whether that transfer is warm, and how recordings reach your existing storage and quality processes.
how does the agent integrate with our contact centre platform, and what does a warm transfer with full context look like?
#### Guardrails, escalation and observability
Production programmes fail on governance more often than on model quality. You need a way to test conversation changes before customers see them, limit what the agent can say and do, set escalation triggers, and find out why one call went wrong. Ask to see the evaluation tooling rather than hear it described, since platforms differ most here and demo it least well.
show us how you test a prompt change before it goes live, and how we would investigate a single failed call.
### Deployment models and compliance requirements
On-premise availability is more common than it was two years ago, and the label covers a wide range of arrangements. Ask which components process raw audio and where those components run, rather than asking whether on-premise exists. Ask whether model weights are included. Where a vendor publishes open weights, you can verify the answer instead of accepting it.
The regime that applies follows from where calls happen and what they carry. India's DPDP Act covers digital personal data collected in India and processing outside India tied to offering goods or services there, though its substantive obligations start in May 2027, so design toward that date. RBI outsourcing rules keep the regulated entity responsible for outsourced activity whatever the vendor arrangement. IRDAI information and cyber security guidelines extend to intermediaries and third-party administrators. US healthcare requires a business associate agreement with vendors that create, receive, maintain or transmit protected health information on a covered entity's behalf.
Outbound calling carries a specific obligation teams often miss. TRAI's amended commercial communications regulations require senders to notify the originating access provider in advance about auto-dialer or robo-call use and to state the intended objective in writing. Revoked consent also triggers a 90-day wait before you can seek it again.
AI disclosure varies more than vendor marketing suggests. The EU AI Act requires from August 2026 that people be told they are interacting with an AI system unless that is obvious. A few US states require proactive disclosure today, and a proposed FCC rule would create a federal requirement, though it remains unfinalised. India has no equivalent rule for real-time voice agents. Most enterprises disclose anyway, which is worth deciding as policy rather than inheriting from a vendor template.
Voiceprints and speaker embeddings count as biometric data under GDPR and under US state laws including Illinois BIPA. India's DPDP Act contains no biometric category at all, so handling them at your highest sensitivity tier is a sound internal standard rather than an Indian legal requirement.
Treat all of this as a checklist for your legal and compliance teams. Vendors can tell you what they support. Whether that satisfies your obligations is a call for your own counsel.
### What this means for your shortlist

What binds you

Kore.ai where a sovereign region or private cloud satisfies your reviewers and you are standardising many use cases at once. Rule out SaaS-only platforms early rather than after a successful pilot.
Insurance

### What an enterprise voice agent programme costs
Published cost-per-contact benchmarks vary so widely by market, channel definition and vintage that none of them survives contact with a finance team. Build the comparison yourself. Take agent time, supervision, infrastructure and attrition, divide by handled volume, then set that against a modelled automated cost at your expected containment rate. Containment matters more than the per-minute rate you negotiate, because a call that escalates costs you the automated attempt and the human handling.
#### The costs that are not on the pricing page
Platform pricing rarely covers the whole programme. Most vendors bill telephony minutes separately, and platforms that let you bring your own models mean you pay the orchestrator alongside each model provider. Engineering time for integration and conversation design usually forms the largest line in year one and almost never appears in a vendor estimate.
Teams overlook tuning most often. Prompts, escalation rules and confidence thresholds all need revisiting as call patterns shift, which is continuing operational work rather than a project that ends.
### How to run a platform bake-off
A structured comparison will tell you more than any number of vendor demos. Budget six to eight weeks rather than four, because assembling and clearing the test data usually takes longer than the technical work.
Choose one use case with a measurable outcome.
Containment rate on a specific inbound query type works well. Avoid starting with your hardest workflow.
Assemble a test set from your own calls.
Aim for 200 to 500 recordings covering your accent range, your noise conditions and your domain vocabulary. De-identify before sharing with any vendor, and start the data processing agreement review on day one, since it usually sets the critical path.
Build the same agent on two or three shortlisted platforms.
Identical prompt, identical escalation rules, identical integrations, so differences reflect the platform rather than the configuration.
Measure the same numbers on each.
End-to-end latency at p95 on your own telephony, entity accuracy, containment, escalation rate and cost per interaction.
Run the security and deployment review alongside it.
Ask the component-level residency question early, since the answer can eliminate an option whatever the results show.
Score against weighted criteria you agreed before testing,
so your requirements decide the outcome rather than the strongest demo.
### How we compiled this comparison
Platform descriptions come from each vendor's public documentation and product pages as of the verification date at the top of this article. Capability statements reflect what each vendor publishes rather than independent testing, and we attribute vendor-published figures for latency, channel counts and integrations as such. Speech recognition benchmark figures for Prisma v2.5 come from Gnani AI's published evaluations on public datasets, with the methodology available separately. Regulatory summaries cite primary sources and are not legal advice.
Several vendors repositioned during 2026. If you represent a platform listed here and something has changed, contact us and we will update the entry.
### Frequently Asked Questions
What is the best AI voice agent platform for enterprise?
It depends on how much of the stack you intend to own and what your security review permits. LiveKit and Pipecat suit teams building their own pipeline. Vapi and Retell suit teams wanting managed orchestration while keeping model choice. Gnani AI, Kore.ai, Uniphore, Observe.AI and Skit.ai deliver full-stack agents, with Gnani AI fitting deployments where the model weights need to run inside your environment.
What is the difference between a voice agent platform and an orchestration tool?
An orchestration tool coordinates the models in a voice agent and manages real-time flow between them, covering turn-taking, interruptions, conversation state and tool calls. A full-stack platform adds the underlying speech and language models, telephony and governance tooling, so you deploy an agent rather than assemble one.
Can we just build on OpenAI's Realtime API?
Realtime handles the conversational loop. A production deployment still needs telephony, conversation state across sessions, integration with your systems, guardrails, escalation logic and observability. Teams taking this route usually pair it with an orchestration framework and should budget for the surrounding layer rather than the model alone.
Can we just use Google CCAI, Microsoft Azure or Amazon Connect?
They work when you have engineering capacity and an existing commitment to that cloud. They give you capable building blocks rather than a packaged agent, so the integration effort resembles building your own pipeline. Judge them against the framework tier rather than against full-stack platforms.
Can voice agents run on-premise?
Several platforms offer it, though the term covers different arrangements. In many cases the application layer deploys locally while model inference still depends on an external provider. Gnani Artha runs the models, the agent platform and the infrastructure inside your environment, with open weights on a single node. Ask any vendor which components process raw audio and where those components run.
Do voice agents have to tell callers they are AI?
It depends on jurisdiction. The EU AI Act requires it from August 2026 unless the AI nature is obvious, a few US states require proactive disclosure, and a proposed FCC rule would create a federal requirement that remains unfinalised. India has no equivalent rule for real-time voice agents. Most enterprises disclose anyway, as policy.
How long does an enterprise voice agent deployment take?
A contained single use case can reach production in four to eight weeks. Broader programmes usually run three to six months, and telephony and CRM integration plus iteration on conversation design drive the timeline more than the initial build.

### TL;DR
Kannada speech to text is harder than English transcription for three reasons: Kannada is agglutinative, so one written word carries what English spreads across several; speakers code-switch into English constantly; and most real audio arrives over 8kHz telephony rather than a clean microphone. Providers fall into four groups, which are the global cloud speech APIs, developer-first transcription APIs, open-source Indic models, and India-native telephony models. Choose by asking for word error rate on noisy 8kHz Kannada audio with code-switching, measured on a public benchmark, because accuracy on clean studio audio predicts almost nothing about accuracy on a real call.
### Why Kannada speech to text is harder than it looks
Kannada has more than 50 million speakers and a written tradition stretching back centuries, and it is poorly served by speech recognition built for English. Three structural problems explain most of the gap.
The first is morphology. Kannada is agglutinative, which means a single written word can carry tense, case, number and politeness where English would use four separate words. A recogniser that treats words as atomic units fragments Kannada badly, and a tokenizer designed for English wastes capacity on every Kannada word it encounters. Gnani AI rebuilt the vocabulary in
Gnani Evon v3.3
around Indian scripts for this reason, at 163,072 tokens, which consumes roughly 20% fewer tokens per Indian word than a general-purpose tokenizer.
The second is code-switching. Kannada speakers move into English mid-sentence as a matter of routine, particularly for numbers, technical terms and anything financial. A system that handles Kannada and English separately, and switches between two models, loses the boundary and with it the sentence. Handling both inside one model is a different engineering problem from supporting both as options.
The third is the channel. Dictation apps are tested on clean 16kHz audio from a microphone held close to the speaker. Contact centres receive 8kHz telephony audio, compressed, often from a moving vehicle or a crowded shop, over a network that drops packets. A word error rate measured on the first condition tells you very little about the second, and vendors do not always say which they measured.

### The four kinds of Kannada speech to text provider
Named products change their specifications often, so treat the groups below as categories to evaluate rather than as a ranked list, and check every published figure against the provider's own current documentation before you rely on it.
#### 1. Global cloud speech APIs
Google Cloud Speech-to-Text, Microsoft Azure Speech Services and Amazon Transcribe all support Kannada, and all three bring a mature ecosystem: documented SDKs, regional availability, billing that finance teams already understand, and integration with the rest of a cloud estate. For a team already committed to one of those clouds, the integration cost is close to zero, and that is a genuine advantage no India-native vendor can match.
The trade-off appears at telephony quality and at scale. These models are trained predominantly on broad multilingual corpora rather than on Indian call audio, and per-minute pricing that is comfortable in a pilot becomes a significant line item across a contact centre running millions of minutes.
#### 2. Developer-first transcription APIs
Providers such as AssemblyAI and Deepgram compete on developer experience: fast onboarding, clean documentation, predictable per-minute pricing and features like diarization exposed without a sales conversation. For a startup that needs transcription working this week, this category is usually the quickest path from signup to a working call.
Indian language depth is the question to press. Ask specifically which Indian languages are production-supported rather than listed, and whether code-switched audio is handled inside a single request.
#### 3. Open-source Indic models
Research groups in India, including work from the IITs, have released open-weight ASR models covering Kannada and other Indian languages. The licence cost is zero, the weights can be inspected, and the model can be fine-tuned on your own data and run entirely inside your own infrastructure. For research, for academic work and for teams with machine learning engineers to spare, that control is worth a great deal.
What you take on is the operational burden. There is no uptime commitment, no support path, no managed scaling and no roadmap, and the engineering time to productionise an open checkpoint is routinely underestimated.
#### 4. India-native telephony models
This group trains on Indian call audio first rather than adapting a global model afterwards.
Gnani Prisma v2.5
sits here, trained on more than 14 million hours of real telephonic audio across 10 or more production Indian languages including Kannada, plus Hinglish, Tanglish and Benglish code-switching. The honest limitation is breadth. A provider focused on Indian languages will not match a global cloud vendor's total language count, so a business transcribing Kannada alongside Polish and Thai needs either a second provider or a different choice.

### How to evaluate Kannada speech to text
Six questions separate a usable evaluation from a demo that proves nothing.
What audio was the word error rate measured on?
Insist on noisy 8kHz telephony audio in Kannada if that is what you will process. Accept no figure without the test condition attached.
Is the benchmark public?
A result on a published benchmark such as Kathbath can be checked. A vendor-internal figure cannot.
How is code-switching handled?
Ask whether Kannada and English are resolved inside one model in one pass, and test it with a recording of someone reading an account number aloud mid-sentence.
What is the streaming latency, and measured how?
Time to first partial transcript and end-to-end latency are different numbers. Gnani AI reports sub-200ms streaming latency for Prisma v2.5.
What concurrency is supported in production?
A contact centre needs thousands of simultaneous streams, not a rate limit sized for a prototype. Gnani AI reports support for 35,000 or more simultaneous streams.
Where can it run?
Cloud, private cloud, on-premise and air-gapped are four different compliance postures, and for regulated audio the deployment option often decides the vendor.
Test with your own audio. Record 50 to 100 real calls across your actual accent range, line quality and background conditions, transcribe them with each candidate, and count the errors on the terms that matter commercially, which are names, amounts, dates and identifiers. A model that scores well overall but mishears account numbers is not fit for a banking workflow.
### Where Gnani Prisma v2.5 fits
Prisma v2.5 is built for the telephony case rather than the dictation case. Alongside the recognition itself it carries speaker diarization, named entity recognition tuned for financial and insurance vocabulary, and domain dictionaries covering terms such as CIBIL, PAN, NEFT, RTGS and UPI, which are exactly the words a general model mangles. Access is available over REST, a realtime WebSocket and batch, and it deploys to cloud, hybrid or on-premise.
Published benchmark detail sits in the

Gnani AI is SOC 2 Type 2 certified and ISO 27001 certified, and HIPAA, GDPR and PCI-DSS compliant. Call recordings, transcripts and call metadata are personal information under the DPDP Act, and speaker embeddings used for voice authentication are biometric data at the highest level of sensitivity. Confirm with your legal and compliance team before deployment.
### Where Kannada speech to text gets used
Four patterns account for most production volume in Karnataka and the wider South Indian market.
Contact centre transcription and quality assurance.
Transcribing every Kannada call lets
Gnani Analytics
score the full corpus rather than a sampled handful, and surface compliance breaches and recurring complaint themes.
Banking and financial services.
Collections, verification and service calls in Kannada depend on recognising amounts, dates and identifiers correctly, which is where domain vocabulary does the work.
Healthcare intake and follow-up.
Appointment and recovery calls in a patient's own language, with the structured record written back automatically.
Government and citizen services.
Kannada-language service lines where the audio must stay inside a controlled environment, which makes on-premise deployment a requirement rather than a preference.
### How to start testing
Assemble a Kannada test set from your own recordings before you talk to any vendor, because that set is the only thing that will tell you the truth. Then run every candidate against it under identical conditions and score on the terms your business cares about.
Developers can review the request formats, streaming protocol and diarization options in the
Gnani AI developer documentation
and start with the free speech to text minutes included on signup. For a walkthrough against your own Kannada call audio and deployment constraints,
book a demo with the Gnani AI team
.
### Frequently asked questions
What is Kannada speech to text and why does it need a specialised model?
Kannada speech to text converts spoken Kannada into written text. It needs a specialised approach because Kannada is agglutinative, so one written word carries what English spreads across several, because speakers code-switch into English mid-sentence as a matter of routine, and because most production audio arrives over compressed 8kHz telephony rather than a clean microphone.
How accurate is Kannada speech to text?
Accuracy depends almost entirely on the audio it was measured against, so a single number means nothing without its test condition. Ask for word error rate on noisy 8kHz Kannada telephony audio with code-switching, measured on a public benchmark. Gnani AI reports under 4% word error rate on Indian speech and 96% code-switching accuracy for Prisma v2.5, and first place in eight of nine Indian languages on Kathbath Noisy 8kHz.
What should a business compare when choosing a Kannada ASR provider?
Six things: the audio condition behind the accuracy figure, whether the benchmark is public, how code-switching is handled inside a single request, streaming latency and how it was measured, supported production concurrency, and which deployment options are available. Test every candidate against 50 to 100 of your own recordings before deciding.
Can Kannada speech to text handle Kannada and English in the same sentence?
It depends on the model. Systems that run Kannada and English as separate models lose the switch point and with it the sentence. Prisma v2.5 handles code-switching inside a single model across Indian languages, including Kannada-English mixing, which is a different capability from supporting both languages as options.
Which industries use Kannada speech to text?
Contact centre transcription and quality assurance, banking and financial services for collections and verification calls, healthcare intake and follow-up, and government citizen service lines. The last group often requires on-premise or air-gapped deployment so that audio never leaves a controlled environment.
Can Kannada audio be transcribed without sending it to a public cloud?
Yes. Prisma v2.5 deploys to cloud, hybrid and on-premise, and Gnani Artha runs the full stack on infrastructure the customer controls, including air-gapped configurations. ### Choosing a text to speech Hindi tool: the short answer
The right text to speech Hindi engine depends on one question: is the audio going down a phone line or into a pair of headphones. For telephony, where audio is compressed to 8 kHz and every hundred milliseconds of delay is audible, pick an engine tested on telephony audio and quote its p95 latency, not its average. For media, e-learning and accessibility, where the audio is played back at full bandwidth and generated in advance, naturalness matters and latency mostly does not. The major cloud providers publish per-character pricing and broad language coverage. India-focused engines train on Indian telephony audio and code-switched Hindi. Neither is automatically better, and any vendor's published quality score, including Gnani AI's, was measured on that vendor's own test set.
The honest version of this comparison is short: shortlist three engines, synthesise the same fifty lines of your own script on each, and listen. Everything below is how to make that test tell you something.
### What makes Hindi hard for text to speech
Hindi is not a hard language for a speech synthesiser in the abstract. It is hard in the ways real Indian businesses actually use it.
Code-switching.
Real sentences mix Devanagari and Latin script, and Hindi and English words, inside one utterance. "Aapka payment due date 15th hai." An engine that switches accents mid-sentence, or reads the English word with an unrelated pronunciation, sounds wrong immediately.
Schwa deletion.
Written Hindi carries inherent vowels that are not pronounced. "नमक" is namak, not namaka. Getting this wrong is the single most common tell of a weak Hindi voice.
Numbers, dates and currency.
An amount, a policy number and a date all need different readings, and the lakh and crore system does not map onto a generic number handler.
Proper nouns.
Indian names, place names and product names are where generic models degrade fastest, and they are exactly what a collections or delivery call is full of.
Telephony bandwidth.
A voice that sounds excellent at 44.1 kHz can sound thin and buzzy once it is downsampled to 8 kHz and pushed through a codec. Most vendor demos are not played at 8 kHz.
### The three things to actually test
#### Naturalness, on your own script
Mean Opinion Score is the standard measure, collected by asking listeners to rate samples from 1 to 5. It is useful and it does not transfer between vendors. Two MOS figures are comparable only when the same listeners rated the same sentences under the same conditions, and vendor-published scores almost never meet that bar. Treat any cross-vendor MOS table, including one on this site, as a starting point for your own test rather than a result.
Run the test on your own copy. Fifty lines from your actual IVR script, including the numbers, the names and the code-switched sentences, will separate engines faster than any published number.
#### Latency, at the percentile that matters
For anything conversational, the figure to ask for is time to first audio byte at p95 or p99, on the audio format you will actually use. An average latency figure hides the tail, and the tail is where calls break. If the vendor quotes an average, ask again.
For batch generation, such as e-learning narration or audiobook production, latency is close to irrelevant and you should optimise for cost per character and voice quality instead.
#### Telephony audio, not studio audio
Ask for samples at 8 kHz, through the codec your carrier uses. This is the test most vendors would rather you skipped, and it is the one that predicts what your customers will hear.
### What the main text to speech Hindi options publish
The table below states only what each vendor publishes on its own pages, checked on 15 September 2026. It deliberately does not score the vendors against each other on quality, because their quality figures were not measured under comparable conditions.

### How to run a fair Hindi TTS comparison
Write the test set first.
Fifty lines of your own copy, covering numbers, dates, currency, at least ten Indian proper nouns, and ten code-switched sentences. Freeze it before you hear any audio.
Generate on every candidate with default settings.
Tuning one engine and not the others is the most common way these comparisons go wrong.
Downsample everything to the format you will ship.
If it is going down a phone line, evaluate at 8 kHz.
Blind the listeners.
Strip the filenames. Use at least ten listeners who are fluent Hindi speakers, and include people who are not on the project.
Rate naturalness and intelligibility separately.
A voice can be pleasant and still mispronounce your product name, and intelligibility is what costs you a repeat call.
Measure latency under load, not on a single request.
Ramp to your expected concurrency and read the p95.
Price the winner on your real volume.
Per-character pricing and per-minute pricing diverge sharply at scale, and a free tier disappears in week one of production.
### Where Gnani AI's Timbre v2.5 sits, honestly
Gnani AI builds
Timbre v2.5
for Indian telephony rather than for media production, and the specification reflects that focus. Gnani AI reports ten production languages including Hindi, Bengali, Kannada, Gujarati, Punjabi, Marathi, Telugu, Tamil, Malayalam and Indian English, with region-specific accent variants. Gnani AI reports a p95 of 242 ms on telephony audio, a MOS of 4.23 measured on 8 kHz telephony audio, and a MOS floor of 4.1 across all ten languages. Those are Gnani AI's own measurements on Gnani AI's own test set, which is exactly the caveat this article applies to every other vendor.
Three things count against it, and you should weigh them.
Gnani AI publishes no list pricing.
The cloud providers publish a per-character rate you can model in a spreadsheet before you speak to anyone. Gnani AI does not, which is a real disadvantage at the evaluation stage. Ask for a written per-character or per-minute rate early.
The language count is narrower than the hyperscalers'.
Ten production languages is the right set for Indian telephony and the wrong set if you need European or East Asian coverage from one vendor.
The model page and the API page disagree.
One states 21 or more languages for Timbre v2.5, the other lists ten. Ask which number applies to the production API before you plan around it.
Where it earns its place is the narrow case it was built for: 8 kHz telephony, code-switched Hindi, and a latency budget that leaves room for a reasoning layer in between. The
model pages
list the full stack, and the
Prisma v2.5 speech recognition page
covers the other half of a voice loop.
### What free Hindi text to speech gets you
Free tools are fine for the job they are actually good at, which is checking whether your text sounds right before you spend money. Browser-based translation tools and open-source synthesisers will read Hindi intelligibly. They will not give you a service level, a p95 latency figure, a commercial licence for the output, or a voice that holds up across a thousand calls a day.
The line is straightforward. Prototyping and internal tools, free is fine. Anything a customer hears, buy a service with terms attached, and read the licence on the generated audio before you ship it.
### Where this leaves you
Pick on your own audio, in your own format, with your own script, rated by people who speak the language. Published scores narrow the shortlist and settle nothing. Ask every vendor for a p95 latency figure on 8 kHz audio and a written rate on your real volume, and treat any vendor that will not give you both as having answered the question.
To run that test against Timbre v2.5 with your own script,
book a demo
,
or start from
the API documentation
.
The
Artha sovereign stack
covers on-premise and air-gapped deployment for teams whose audio cannot leave their own environment, and the
product overview
covers where synthesis sits inside a full voice agent.
### Frequently Asked Questions
What is the best text to speech Hindi tool?
There is no single best one, and any article that names one without knowing your channel is guessing. For telephony and conversational use, pick an engine tested on 8 kHz audio that publishes a p95 latency figure. For media, e-learning and accessibility, pick on naturalness and per-character cost. Shortlist three, synthesise fifty lines of your own script on each, and have fluent Hindi speakers rate the output blind.
Is Google Translate good enough for Hindi text to speech?
For checking pronunciation and prototyping, yes. For production, no, and not mainly for quality reasons. The web translation interface is not a supported production API, it offers no service level, no latency guarantee and no concurrency commitment, and the terms of use on the generated audio are not written for commercial redistribution. Google publishes a separate, properly supported Cloud Text-to-Speech API for production use, with published per-character pricing.
How much does Hindi text to speech cost?
Published per-character pricing from the major cloud vendors, checked on 15 September 2026, runs from around 4 US dollars per million characters for their basic voice tiers to 30 US dollars per million for their newest high-definition voices, with some premium tiers considerably higher. India-focused vendors including Gnani AI generally quote rather than publish, so you have to ask. Model the cost on your real monthly character volume rather than on a free tier, because the free tier is gone by the end of the first month of production.
What is a good MOS score for Hindi text to speech?
Above 4.0 on a 5-point scale usually means listeners describe the voice as natural rather than as a good synthetic voice. The number matters less than the conditions. A MOS collected on full-bandwidth studio audio tells you almost nothing about how the same voice sounds at 8 kHz on a phone call, and scores from two vendors were almost never collected from the same listeners on the same sentences, so they do not compare directly.
Can Hindi text to speech handle mixed Hindi and English sentences?
Some engines handle it well and most demos avoid testing it. Code-switching inside a single sentence is the normal case in Indian business conversation and it is where engines diverge most. Put at least ten code-switched sentences from your own script into the test set, and listen specifically for whether the accent shifts mid-sentence when the engine crosses from Hindi to English.
Do I need a different engine for phone calls than for videos?
Often, yes. Telephony compresses audio to 8 kHz and demands a low p95 latency, so it rewards engines trained on telephony audio. Media playback is full bandwidth and usually generated ahead of time, so it rewards naturalness and cost per character. An engine tuned for one is not automatically wrong for the other, but it is worth testing separately rather than assuming a single winner.

### ASR vs STT: the short answer
ASR vs STT is a naming difference far more often than it is a technology difference. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) is the research and engineering term for the task of turning audio of human speech into text. Speech to text (STT) is the product and API term for the same task. When a vendor sells you an STT API, the thing running inside it is an ASR model. When a paper benchmarks an ASR system, the output it scores is text.
The distinction starts to matter in two situations. The first is when ASR is used to describe a full recognition stack rather than a single transcription call. The second is when a procurement document uses the two terms as if they named different products, which turns a vocabulary question into a scoping question. Both are worth ten minutes of your time before an RFP goes out.
### Where the two terms come from
Automatic speech recognition is the older label. It belongs to the academic lineage of speech processing, where the task has always been framed as recognition: given an acoustic signal, recover the sequence of words that produced it. Conference papers, benchmark leaderboards and model cards use ASR because that is the name of the problem being solved.
Speech to text arrived with the cloud API era. It describes what the buyer gets rather than what the system does, and it reads cleanly in a product catalogue next to text to speech. Major cloud providers market their transcription services under the speech to text label, which is why the term dominates developer documentation and pricing pages while ASR dominates the literature.
Neither term is more correct. They sit at different layers of the same stack, and the layer you are standing on decides which one you reach for.
### Where the ASR vs STT distinction has technical substance
There is a real engineering sense in which ASR is the wider word. A production speech system does more than emit a string of words, and the extra capabilities usually live under the ASR label rather than the STT one.
Consider what a contact centre actually needs from a recognition stack. It needs the words, but it also needs to know who spoke them, which is diarization. It needs timestamps so a transcript can be aligned to audio for review. It needs entity recognition so that an account number, a policy reference or a payment amount is captured as a structured field rather than a run of digits. It needs domain vocabulary so that terms specific to lending, insurance or telecom are recognised rather than approximated. It needs confidence scores so that downstream automation can decide when to act and when to escalate.
A minimal STT endpoint returns text. A recognition stack returns text plus the structure that makes the text usable.
Gnani Prisma v2.5
is sold through a speech to text API and carries diarization, named entity recognition tuned for financial and insurance terminology, and configurable domain vocabulary covering identifiers such as CIBIL, PAN, Aadhaar, NEFT, RTGS and UPI. The product name says STT. The capability set is ASR in the fuller sense.
### How the terms are used in products, research and procurement
Three contexts account for almost every appearance of either term, and each has its own convention. Reading a document correctly means knowing which context you are in.
Research and benchmarking use ASR. Word error rate, the standard accuracy measure, is reported against ASR systems, and public test sets are described as ASR benchmarks. Gnani AI reports Prisma v2.5 under 4% WER on Indian speech and a first place in eight of nine Indian languages on the Kathbath Noisy 8kHz benchmark, figures published on
the Gnani AI models page
and expanded in the
Prisma v2.5 benchmark write-up
.
Product catalogues and developer documentation use STT. The endpoint is named for the transformation it performs, and it sits beside a text to speech endpoint for symmetry.
Procurement documents use both, often in the same paragraph, and this is where the confusion costs money. A requirements list that asks separately for an ASR engine and an STT API invites vendors to quote two line items for one capability.

### Why Indian language audio changes the calculation
The ASR vs STT question gets sharper in Indian deployments, because the gap between a generic transcription call and a tuned recognition stack is widest exactly where Indian telephony lives.
Three conditions drive that gap. Telephone audio is narrowband, typically 8kHz, and carries codec artefacts that studio-trained models have never encountered. Speakers code-switch inside a single sentence, mixing English with Hindi, Tamil or Bengali in patterns that a monolingual model cannot segment. Dialectal and accent variation across regions is wide enough that a model trained on one variety degrades noticeably on another.
A system that handles these conditions has to be trained on them. Gnani AI reports that Prisma v2.5 was trained on 14M+ hours of real telephonic audio and supports 10+ production languages alongside Hinglish, Tanglish and Benglish code-switching, with 96% code-switching accuracy. Whether that stack is labelled ASR or STT on the invoice changes nothing about what it does. What changes everything is whether the training data resembles the audio you intend to send it. The
State of ASR Models 2026
report sets out how these conditions separate systems that look equivalent on paper.
### What ASR vs STT means for BFSI and contact centre buyers
If you are writing a requirements document, stop treating ASR vs STT as a product distinction and start specifying capabilities. The questions that separate vendors are not about terminology.
What audio was the model trained on, and does it match your channel conditions?
Does the system return diarization, timestamps, entities and confidence scores, or only a transcript?
Can domain vocabulary be configured for your products and identifiers?
What are the streaming latency characteristics, and what concurrency is supported?
Which deployment modes are available, and do they satisfy your data residency obligations?
That last question carries regulatory weight in Indian financial services. Conversation audio, transcripts and call metadata are personal data under the DPDP Act, and BFSI deployments sit under RBI expectations while insurance deployments sit under IRDAI. Gnani AI offers cloud, private cloud, on-premise and air-gapped deployment, and
Gnani Artha
describes the sovereign configuration where the stack runs on infrastructure the customer controls. Confirm with your legal and compliance team before deployment.
Downstream of recognition, the transcript is the input to everything else.
Gnani Analytics
scores quality and flags compliance issues across the corpus,
Gnani Assist
retrieves policy answers mid-call, and
the Gnani AI enterprise platform
runs the conversations themselves. A weak recognition layer degrades all three, which is the practical reason the engineering question deserves more attention than the naming one.
### The ASR vs STT distinction worth remembering
Treat ASR as the name of the problem and STT as the name of the product that solves it. When someone uses ASR to mean a recognition stack with diarization, entities and domain tuning, and STT to mean a plain transcription call, that is a useful shorthand rather than a formal taxonomy, and it is worth confirming rather than assuming.
In an RFP, write one capability line and describe what the output must contain. In a benchmark discussion, use ASR and name the test set. In a developer conversation, use STT and name the endpoint. The ASR vs STT question has a short answer, and the long answers that follow it are the ones that decide whether a deployment works. Start with
the Gnani AI developer documentation
if you want to test the difference against your own audio, or
book a demo
to walk through a deployment.
### Frequently asked questions
Is ASR the same as STT?
In almost every practical case, yes. Automatic speech recognition is the research term for the task of turning speech into text, and speech to text is the product term for the same task. The exception is when ASR is used to mean a full recognition stack that also returns diarization, timestamps, entities and confidence scores, while STT means a plain transcription call. If a document draws that line, confirm it rather than assuming it.
Which term should I use in an RFP?
Use one capability line and describe the output rather than the label. Asking separately for an ASR engine and an STT API invites vendors to quote two line items for one capability. Specify what the response must contain, what audio conditions the model must handle, what streaming latency and concurrency you need, and which deployment modes satisfy your data residency obligations.
What is the difference between ASR, STT and NLU?
ASR and STT both name the step that turns audio into text. Natural language understanding is the step after it, which takes that text and extracts intent, entities and meaning. A voice agent needs both: recognition to hear the words, understanding to decide what to do about them. A weak recognition layer limits how well the understanding layer can perform, because it only ever sees the transcript.
Does a speech to text API always run an ASR model underneath?
Yes. The API is the interface and the ASR model is the engine behind it. What differs between vendors is whether that model is proprietary or a wrapped third party, what audio it was trained on, and whether it can be tuned for your domain vocabulary. Gnani AI reports that Prisma v2.5 is built in house and trained on 14M+ hours of real telephonic audio.
Why does ASR accuracy drop on Indian telephony audio?
Three conditions work against models trained on clean studio English. Telephone audio is narrowband, typically 8kHz, with codec artefacts. Speakers code-switch between English and an Indian language inside a single sentence. Dialect and accent vary widely across regions. A model has to be trained on audio with these properties to handle them, which is why training data composition matters more than the ASR or STT label on the product.

## What Is Hinglish and Why Speech Recognition Fails on Code-Switching

### What Hinglish is, and why speech recognition keeps failing on it
TL;DR:
Hinglish is the mixing of Hindi and English inside a single conversation, and often inside a single sentence, as in "aapka loan amount disburse ho gaya hai, so please check karo apna account". It is the normal register for urban and semi-urban India in professional settings. Most speech recognition systems break on it because they identify the language once at the start of an utterance and hold that assumption for the whole segment. When the switch happens mid-clause, the audio is scored against the wrong phoneme inventory and the wrong vocabulary distribution at the same time, so words from the second language are substituted or deleted.
That failure is invisible in a vendor demo, because demos use clean monolingual audio. It shows up three weeks into production, in a compliance review, when a transcript of a collections call cannot be used as a record.
### Hinglish is a register, not an error
Code-switching is the alternation between two or more languages within one conversation. Linguists have studied it for decades, and the finding that matters here is that it correlates with fluency rather than with deficiency. A speaker who moves cleanly between Hindi and English mid-sentence is demonstrating command of both.
Two forms behave very differently in front of a recogniser.
Inter-sentential switching
puts the switch at a sentence boundary. "Aapka account verify ho gaya. Your application has been processed." There is an acoustic break, a pause, and a clean reset point. Most recognisers handle this acceptably.
Intra-sentential switching
puts the switch inside the clause. "Aapka loan amount disburse ho gaya hai, so please check karo apna account." There is no boundary and no pause. This is where systems fail, and it is by far the more common form in Indian contact centre speech.
Speech to text
2,000 free STT minutes.
Gnani Prisma v2.5 · Trained on 1M hours of audio · Best in class multi-lingual, multi-speaker
Start building
### Three failures that happen at once
A speech recognition system has an acoustic model that maps audio to phonemes and a language model that scores which word sequences are plausible. On intra-sentential Hinglish, three things go wrong simultaneously.
Failure
Where it happens
What appears in the transcript
What fixes it
Phoneme inventory mismatch
Acoustic model, at the switch point
Substitutions on switched-language words, often phonetically close and semantically wrong
Joint multilingual acoustic modelling trained on code-mixed audio, not two monolingual models
Vocabulary distribution shift
Language model, on English nouns inside Hindi structure
The nearest known word replaces the spoken one, or the word is dropped entirely
Language model trained on the mixed register, plus domain vocabulary for financial terms
Utterance-level language ID
Before transcription begins, once per segment
Systematic errors across the whole segment after the first switch
Frame-level language identification that updates continuously across the utterance
Noise and prior interaction
Decoder, on 8kHz compressed telephony
Errors concentrated on the secondary language rather than spread evenly
Training on real telephony audio at 8kHz rather than on clean studio corpora
Performance figures cited in this article are reported by Gnani AI on its published model and API pages, measured on noisy 8kHz telephony. Word error rates measured on clean 16kHz audio do not compare directly.
#### The phoneme inventory changes mid-sentence
Hindi carries retroflex consonants and aspirated stops that English does not use contrastively. English carries phonemes that standard Hindi does not have. A model committed to one inventory has to approximate everything from the other, and approximation in a decoder becomes substitution in the transcript.
#### The vocabulary distribution shifts
Language models assign probabilities learned from a training corpus. An English noun sitting inside Hindi grammatical structure has very little probability mass in either a Hindi corpus or an English corpus, because neither contains that construction. The decoder resolves the low-probability region by substituting the nearest-sounding word it does know, or by dropping it.
#### Language identification was designed for monolingual speech
This is the architectural root of the problem. Utterance-level language identification makes one decision per segment, before transcription, and is computationally cheap for exactly that reason. It was built for a world where one utterance means one language. Intra-sentential switching violates that assumption by design, so the system does not recover gracefully; it was never given the chance to change its mind.
### Noise makes it worse in a specific direction
Indian contact centre audio arrives at 8kHz, through GSM compression, often from a basic handset in a noisy room. Noise reduces the acoustic model's confidence, and a decoder with low acoustic confidence leans harder on language model priors.
Those priors point toward whichever language dominated training. The result is directional rather than random: on noisy code-switched telephony, errors concentrate on the secondary language. Words from the minority language in the sentence are deleted or replaced at a higher rate than chance would produce. That is why a system can report a respectable overall error rate and still be useless for extracting an amount, a date or a consent statement.
Training data is the only real fix.
Gnani Prisma v2.5
is trained on 14M+ hours of real telephonic audio rather than on clean corpora, and Gnani AI reports under 4% word error rate on Indian speech, 96% code-switching accuracy, and a first-place result in 8 of 9 Indian languages on the Kathbath Noisy 8kHz benchmark. Those figures are measured on noisy 8kHz telephony, so they are not comparable to a word error rate quoted on clean 16kHz studio audio. If you are new to the metric itself,
word error rate explained
covers how it is calculated and what it hides.
### Frame-level language identification is the architectural difference
The variable that separates systems that handle Hinglish from systems that do not is when the language decision gets made.
Utterance-level identification decides once, up front, for the whole segment. Frame-level and jointly trained multilingual modelling updates the language assumption continuously across short windows as the audio unfolds, closer to how a bilingual listener tracks a sentence. It costs more compute and it requires training data that actually contains code-mixed speech.
That second requirement is the one vendors most often gloss over. A model trained on a large Hindi corpus and a large English corpus separately will not automatically transfer to code-mixed speech, because mixing patterns, borrowed vocabulary, Hindi-adapted English phonology and the grammatical frames that host the switch appear in neither corpus. Contact centre training data is the core technical requirement for Indian enterprise speech recognition, not an optional extra. The full model line and the benchmarks behind it sit on the
Gnani AI models page
.
### Beyond Hinglish: the other pairs that matter
Hindi and English is the largest pair by volume, not the only one.
Tanglish (Tamil and English).
Tamil's agglutinative morphology produces hybrid forms where English stems take Tamil suffixes, which defeats vocabulary lookup as well as phoneme mapping.
Kanglish (Kannada and English).
Heavily present in Bengaluru technology and financial services conversations.
Telglish (Telugu and English).
Common across Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.
Benglish (Bengali and English)
, along with Malayalam, Marathi, Gujarati, Punjabi, Odia and Assamese mixing with English, each with its own borrowing patterns.
Prisma v2.5 runs 10+ Indic languages in production and is trained on Hinglish, Tanglish and Benglish code-switching specifically. Coverage of a language on its own does not imply coverage of that language mixed with English, and the two should be evaluated separately.
### How to test an STT API for code-switching before you deploy
Vendor benchmarks will not answer this question for you, because almost nobody publishes error rates on code-mixed audio. Run your own evaluation.
Build a test set from 100 to 200 of your own production calls
, drawn from the regions and campaigns you actually run. De-identify them before they leave your environment. Never send unredacted customer audio to a vendor.
Segment by switching type.
Score inter-sentential and intra-sentential segments separately. A single blended number hides the failure, because intra-sentential accuracy will be materially worse and that is the segment you care about.
Score the entities, not just the words.
Amounts, account references, dates and consent statements carry the business value of the transcript. A 5% error rate that lands entirely on those fields is worse than a 10% rate spread across filler words.
Use telephony-grade audio.
Test at 8kHz through the codec your carrier actually uses. Clean recordings will not show you the noise interaction described above.
Ask for the error type breakdown.
Substitutions and deletions have different downstream consequences. Deletions on a secondary-language amount are the ones that create disputed records.
Ask two architecture questions.
Is language identification utterance-level or frame-level, and what proportion of the training corpus is genuinely code-mixed rather than two monolingual sets combined.
### What it costs when this goes wrong
In collections, an agent saying "teen hazaar rupay ka payment Friday tak" and a transcript recording "teen rupay ka payment" is a three-order-of-magnitude error on a promise to pay, written into the CRM as fact. Deployments running
collections voice AI
depend on that field being right.
In compliance, a disclosure statement delivered in mixed language and transcribed partially leaves you with a call recording that cannot serve as evidence the disclosure happened. Automated quality and compliance scoring through
Gnani Analytics
inherits every transcription error underneath it, so recognition accuracy sets the ceiling for everything built on top.
In voice agents, a dropped English word inside a Hindi sentence breaks intent detection outright, and the customer hears a bot that did not understand a perfectly clear request.
Gnani Agents
handles the conversation layer, and it is only as good as the transcript it receives.
Where data residency governs the deployment, under the DPDP Act and under RBI and IRDAI rules,
Gnani Artha
runs the same stack on-premise or air-gapped so the audio never leaves the customer's network. Confirm with your legal and compliance team before deployment.
### What to do next
Hinglish is not going away, because mixed-language speech is how bilingual people talk. The gap between a compliance-grade transcript and a disputed one, on the same audio, comes down to whether the recognition system was built for monolingual speech with Indic support added afterwards, or trained on code-mixed telephony from the start.
Test on your own audio, under your own noise conditions, before you commit. You can run Hinglish samples against Prisma v2.5 using the
Gnani AI developer documentation
, or
arrange a benchmark with the Gnani AI team
using a de-identified set from your own contact centre.
### Frequently asked questions
What is Hinglish?
Hinglish is the mixing of Hindi and English within one conversation, and frequently within one sentence. It is the standard register for professional and semi-formal communication across urban and semi-urban India. A sentence like "aapka payment due date 15 tareekh hai" is Hinglish, with English nouns carried inside Hindi grammatical structure.
What is code-switching in speech recognition?
Code-switching is alternation between two or more languages in a single conversation. In speech recognition it matters because most systems assume one language per utterance. The common Indian pairs are Hindi and English, Tamil and English, Kannada and English, Telugu and English, and Bengali and English.
Why do most speech recognition APIs fail on Hinglish?
Because they use utterance-level language identification, committing to one language before transcription begins. When the switch happens mid-clause, the audio is decoded against the wrong phoneme inventory and the wrong vocabulary distribution, producing substitutions and deletions on the switched-language words.
Does background noise make code-switching accuracy worse?
Yes, and in a predictable direction. Noise lowers acoustic confidence, which makes the decoder lean on language model priors. Those priors favour the dominant training language, so errors concentrate on the secondary language in the sentence rather than spreading evenly.
Is Hinglish the only code-switching problem in India?
No. Tanglish, Kanglish, Telglish and Benglish present the same architectural problem with different phonological and vocabulary patterns. An engine that handles Hinglish well has not necessarily been trained on Tamil and English mixing, so each pair needs separate evaluation.
How do I test a vendor's Hinglish accuracy before signing?
Build a de-identified test set from your own production calls, score inter-sentential and intra-sentential segments separately, evaluate accuracy on amounts, dates and consent statements rather than on overall word error rate, run it at 8kHz through your own codec, and ask whether language identification is utterance-level or frame-level.

### Real-time transcription and batch transcription are different products
Teams evaluating speech to text usually compare vendors on accuracy, language coverage and price. The choice that decides more is the one they skip: whether the transcript arrives during the call or after it. Real-time transcription and batch transcription are not the same engine running at two speeds. They have different accuracy profiles, different infrastructure demands and different failure modes.
TL;DR:
Real-time transcription streams audio to the speech engine over a persistent connection and returns text within milliseconds, which is what live agent assist, in-call compliance alerting and voice bots require. Batch transcription runs after the call ends, sees the whole recording before producing output, and is more accurate because it can use context from both directions. Most contact centres need both: batch for post-call analytics and quality monitoring, real-time for the specific flows where value depends on acting during the conversation.
Gnani Prisma v2.5
supports REST, realtime WebSocket and batch on the same model, with sub-200ms streaming latency.
### What real-time transcription actually means
Streaming transcription sends audio to the engine as it arrives and returns text continuously over a WebSocket connection. The number that matters is P95 latency, measured from speech to returned text, because a system that is fast on average and slow one call in ten is useless for agent assist.
Streaming engines emit two kinds of output. Partial transcripts arrive fast and change as more audio comes in. Final transcripts are stable and arrive slightly later. Applications that render partials to a human need to handle text that rewrites itself, which is an interface problem as much as an engineering one.
Sub-200ms is the threshold below which live agent assist and voice bots behave naturally.
streams under 200ms and supports 35,000+ simultaneous streams, which is the constraint that usually bites at contact centre scale rather than single-stream latency.
### What batch transcription actually means
Batch processing takes the completed recording and transcribes it as one job. Because the model sees the full audio before committing to any output, it can use context from later in the call to resolve something ambiguous earlier. That bidirectional context is why batch is more accurate on the same audio.
Batch is also simpler to run. No persistent connections to manage, no partial transcript state, no reconnection logic when the network drops mid-call. For a first deployment this matters more than teams expect.

### Comparing the two modes
The trade-offs line up predictably once you separate them out.
