### TL;DR
Voice authentication for banks verifies a caller from the characteristics of their voice rather than from something they know or something they carry. It runs in two modes: active, where the caller speaks a passphrase, and passive, where the system verifies from natural conversation while the call proceeds. The operational win is removing knowledge-based verification questions from the front of every call, which shortens handle time and closes the social engineering path that those questions create. The risk that decides the procurement is synthetic speech, so liveness and anti-spoof detection matter more than raw accuracy numbers. Voiceprints are biometric data under Indian law, and the storage and consent design belongs in the project from day one rather than at the end.
### How voice authentication works in a bank
A voice authentication system builds a mathematical representation of a speaker from an enrolment sample, stores that representation, and compares later audio against it. The representation captures both physical characteristics, which come from the shape of the vocal tract, and behavioural ones, which come from rhythm, pace and pronunciation. Gnani AI reports that
Gnani Biometrics
extracts 300+ voice features per call and supports cross-lingual enrolment, meaning a customer enrolled speaking one language can be verified speaking another.
That last property matters more in India than it does in most markets. A customer may enrol in Hindi and call back in Kannada, or switch language mid-call, and a system that treats those as different speakers will fail exactly the customers it was bought to serve.
The comparison produces a score rather than a yes or no, and the bank sets the threshold. A high threshold rejects more genuine customers. A low one admits more impostors. Where you set it is a business decision about which error costs more in a given call type, and it should differ between a balance enquiry and a funds transfer.
ENTERPRISE VOICE AI
See Gnani AI's Voice AI Agent in action
200+ Enterprises · 30M daily calls · 10 Indic languages
Book A Demo
### Active and passive voice authentication compared
The enrolment mode is the first real design decision, and it shapes the customer experience more than the underlying model does.
Dimension
Active voice authentication
Passive voice authentication
What the customer does
Speaks a set passphrase
Nothing beyond talking normally
Enrolment friction
Explicit enrolment step, easy to explain, easy to refuse
Enrolment can happen during ordinary calls, with consent
Where it fits
High-value transaction confirmation, step-up checks
Contact centre verification at the start of every call
Audio needed to verify
A short fixed utterance
A few seconds of natural conversation
Main weakness
A fixed phrase is a fixed target for replay and cloning
Depends more heavily on line quality and background noise
Customer perception
Visible security, reads as deliberate
Invisible, so the consent conversation has to do more work
Fallback still required
Yes
Most banks that deploy at scale end up passive for the contact centre and active for high-value transaction confirmation, using the passphrase as a deliberate friction point where friction is appropriate.
### What voice authentication actually defends against
It closes one specific attack path well. Knowledge-based verification asks for information that is frequently available to an attacker: date of birth, address, last transaction, mother's maiden name. An attacker who has collected that information passes the check, and the genuine customer who has forgotten one detail fails it. Removing the questions removes both problems at once.
Gnani AI reports sub-second passive verification, under 5 seconds to verify identity, a 40-second reduction in average handle time and a 99%+ fraud detection rate for Gnani Biometrics on its own enterprise page. Those are vendor-stated figures measured on Gnani AI deployments, and a detection rate depends entirely on the threshold and the attack mix behind it, so ask any vendor including this one to state both before you compare two numbers.
What it does not defend against is a genuine customer being manipulated into making the call themselves. Authorised push payment fraud survives perfect authentication, because the person on the line is who they claim to be. Voice authentication is a control on impersonation, and it should be sold internally as that rather than as fraud prevention generally.
### Spoofing, deepfakes and liveness
Synthetic speech is the reason this technology needs re-evaluating on a shorter cycle than most security controls. Voice cloning from a short sample is widely available, which means a system that only compares a voiceprint is checking whether the audio sounds like the customer rather than whether a person spoke it.
Anti-spoof and liveness detection are the countermeasure, and they work by looking for the artefacts that recorded or generated audio carries and live speech does not. Gnani AI lists anti-spoof and deepfake detection as part of Gnani Biometrics rather than as an add-on, which is the right architecture, because a spoof check that can be procured separately can also be descoped separately.
For procurement, the question to ask is not whether a vendor detects deepfakes. Every vendor says yes. Ask what their detection was tested against, how recently, and what happens to the detection rate when a generation method they have not seen appears. A vendor who answers that question specifically is telling you something. One who answers with a percentage is not.
### Accessibility and the fallback path
A voice authentication rollout needs a route for customers it cannot serve. Speech disabilities, severe illness, and the ordinary voice changes that come with age all affect verification. So do heavy background noise and a poor line, neither of which is the customer's fault.
Design the fallback before the launch rather than after the first complaint, and make sure it does not become the soft entry point that attackers use instead. A fallback that reverts to the same knowledge-based questions you removed has reopened the door you just closed.
### What to test before you procure voice authentication
Run it on your own call audio, redacted of identifiers, across your real line conditions rather than on the vendor's sample set.
Test enrolment and verification in different languages for the same speaker, if your customers switch languages. Ask for cross-lingual results specifically.
Ask for false accept and false reject rates at a stated threshold, and insist on both numbers together. One without the other is not a measurement.
Test against synthetic audio you generate yourself, including from a recent cloning tool the vendor was not told about.
Measure the enrolment drop-off rate, because a system nobody enrols in protects nobody.
Establish where the voiceprints are stored, in what form, and what it takes to delete one on request.
Check the deployment options against your own constraints. Gnani AI publishes four modes: cloud, private cloud, on-premise and air-gapped, which matters when biometric data cannot leave the bank's network.
The underlying speech stack is worth examining too, because verification quality depends on audio handling. Gnani AI reports that
Prisma v2.5
is trained on 14M+ hours of real telephonic audio and covers 10+ Indian languages in production. The full model line-up sits on the
models page
, and for banks that need the stack inside their own infrastructure, the
Artha sovereign stack
describes the on-premise deployment. Related use cases sit on the
solutions overview
.
### Voiceprints are biometric data: what that means in India
This is the part that most often gets treated as a late-stage legal review and should not be. A voiceprint is a speaker embedding, and it is biometric personal data. Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, processing it requires a lawful basis, a clearly stated purpose and a retention limit, and the customer's rights over it include correction and erasure. An enrolment consent flow that buries the biometric element in general terms is unlikely to survive scrutiny.
For banks specifically, RBI guidance on authentication and on customer data applies on top, and any outbound contact that forms part of the enrolment campaign sits under TRAI consent and DND rules. Call recordings and transcripts created along the way are personal data in their own right, with their own retention clock.
Gnani AI is SOC 2 Type 2 certified and ISO 27001 certified, and HIPAA, GDPR and PCI-DSS compliant, as published on its own security material. Certification scope is a question to put to any vendor directly rather than to infer from a badge. Confirm with your legal and compliance team before deployment.
### Frequently asked questions
What is the best voice authentication method for banks?
Passive verification for the contact centre, with active passphrase confirmation reserved for high-value transactions, suits most banks. Passive removes the verification questions from the front of every call without asking the customer to do anything, and the active step adds deliberate friction at the point where friction is appropriate. The right threshold differs by call type, so treat it as a per-journey setting rather than a single global number.
How secure is voice authentication compared with PINs and security questions?
It closes the specific weakness that knowledge-based checks have, which is that the answers are often obtainable by an attacker and forgettable by the customer. It introduces a different weakness, which is synthetic speech, and that one is addressed by liveness and anti-spoof detection rather than by the voiceprint comparison itself. A bank comparing the two should compare the attack paths, not the accuracy percentages.
Can voice authentication be fooled by a recording or an AI voice clone?
A system that only compares a voiceprint can be, which is why liveness and anti-spoof detection are not optional components. Ask vendors what their detection has been tested against and how recently, and run your own test with synthetic audio you generate, using a tool the vendor was not told about in advance. Treat this as a control that needs re-testing on a regular cycle rather than a one-time procurement check.
Does voice authentication work across Indian languages?
It works if the system supports cross-lingual enrolment, meaning a customer enrolled in one language can verify in another. Gnani AI lists cross-lingual enrolment as a capability of Gnani Biometrics. Test it with your own speakers switching languages, because this is exactly the case that separates a system built for Indian telephony from one adapted to it.
What happens to customers who cannot use voice authentication?
They need a fallback route, and it needs designing before launch. Speech disabilities, illness, ageing voices, background noise and poor lines all affect verification, and none of them is the customer's fault. The design constraint is that the fallback must not reopen the weakness you removed, so reverting to the same knowledge-based questions is not an acceptable answer.
Is a voiceprint personal data under Indian law?
Yes, and it is biometric personal data, which carries a higher bar than an ordinary customer record. Processing it under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act requires a lawful basis, a stated purpose and a retention limit, and the consent flow needs to make the biometric element explicit rather than bundling it into general terms. RBI guidance applies on top for banks. Confirm with your legal and compliance team before deployment, and if you want to see enrolment and verification running against your own call conditions.

### Voice authentication banking: the short answer
Voice authentication in banking verifies a caller from the sound of their voice instead of a one-time password, a PIN or a security question. The reason banks are moving is not novelty. It is that knowledge-based authentication has become the weakest link in the contact centre, and every second spent on it is a second the agent is not spending on the reason for the call.
### Why one-time passwords stopped being enough
The one-time password was designed for a world where the phone number was a reliable proxy for the person. It no longer is.
A SIM swap moves the number to an attacker without the customer knowing. Malware on the handset reads the message. Social engineering persuades the customer to read the code aloud to someone claiming to be from the bank. None of these are exotic. They are the standard playbook in account takeover.
There is a second problem that shows up in operations rather than in fraud reports. Authentication by question and code takes time on every single call, and it takes it from the front of the call when the customer is least patient. The customer switches app, reads a code, misreads a digit, asks the agent to resend. The call has not started yet.
Voice authentication banking flips the order. Verification happens inside the first exchange of the conversation, while the caller is explaining why they rang.

The process has two halves, enrolment and verification.

extracts 300+ voice features per call and supports cross-lingual enrolment, so a customer who enrols speaking Hindi can be verified later speaking English. Enrolment can be passive, meaning it happens during an ordinary service call rather than in a separate registration step.

compares the live speech against the stored voiceprint and returns a score. ### Anti-spoofing and deepfake detection
The obvious objection to voice authentication is synthetic speech. If a text to speech model can clone a voice from a few seconds of audio, what stops an attacker cloning a customer?
The answer is that a cloned voice and a live human voice are not acoustically identical, and the difference is detectable. Gnani Biometrics publishes anti-spoof and deepfake detection as part of the product rather than as an add-on, covering synthetic speech, replayed recordings and mimicry attempts.
Two things follow for a bank evaluating this. Second, ask how the system behaves when it is unsure. A biometric system that never abstains is a system that will eventually authenticate an attacker, and the correct behaviour on a borderline score is to step up to a second factor, not to guess.

Contact centre authentication.

Self-service and IVR.

A voiceprint is biometric data. Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act it sits in the most sensitive category a bank handles, alongside the identifiers it already protects most carefully. That has practical consequences for the deployment rather than for the pitch.

### Frequently asked questions
What is voice biometrics in banking?
Voice biometrics in banking is the use of a customer's voice as an identity credential, verified against a stored voiceprint rather than against a password or a one-time code. The voiceprint is a mathematical representation of speech characteristics, not a stored recording of the customer. Banks use it to authenticate callers in the contact centre and in self-service channels, usually alongside other controls rather than replacing them entirely.
How does voice authentication work in a bank?
It works in two stages. The bank enrols the customer once, capturing a voiceprint from their speech, which can happen passively during an ordinary service call. On later calls the system compares live speech against that voiceprint and returns a match score in the background while the conversation continues. Gnani AI reports sub-second passive verification and identification in under five seconds. If the score is borderline, a well-designed system steps up to a second factor rather than deciding on its own.
Can voice authentication be fooled by a deepfake?
A cloned voice is a real attack vector, which is why anti-spoof detection is part of the system rather than an optional extra. Synthetic speech, replayed recordings and mimicry leave acoustic traces that differ from live human speech, and Gnani Biometrics publishes detection for all three. The honest caveat is that detection is an arms race, so the right questions for a vendor are how detection is tested on your own audio conditions and how the system behaves when it is uncertain, not whether it is perfect.
Is voice authentication banking legal in India?
Voice authentication is used by banks in India, and a voiceprint is treated as biometric data under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, which places specific obligations on consent, storage, residency and deletion. Practically that means explicit and recorded consent, an alternative authentication route for customers who decline, and a deployment architecture that satisfies the bank's residency position. RBI guidance applies to the banking deployment and TRAI rules apply to any outbound calling built on it. Confirm the specifics with your legal and compliance team before deployment.
Voice biometrics or OTP, which is more secure for a bank?
They fail differently, which is the useful way to think about it. A one-time password is vulnerable to SIM swap, message interception and social engineering, because it protects a channel rather than a person. Voice biometrics is vulnerable to high-quality synthetic speech, which is why spoof detection matters. Most banks end up running both, using voice to remove friction from routine calls and keeping a second factor for high-value transactions.
How long does a voice authentication deployment take?
The variable that dominates is not the technology but enrolment. Verification works from the first enrolled call, so the useful measure is how quickly the enrolled share of your calling base grows, and passive enrolment during ordinary service calls is what makes that curve steep rather than flat. Start with one queue, measure against a control group on the same call types, and expand once the false reject rate on your own audio is understood.

### Deepfake detection in voice biometrics, explained for enterprise teams
Synthetic speech is cheap to produce and hard to hear. A fraudster no longer needs a recording of your customer reading a passphrase. A short clip from a voice note or a webinar is enough raw material for a cloned voice that can hold a conversation with a contact centre agent. Deepfake detection is the layer that decides whether the voice on the line was produced by a person or by a model.
TL;DR:
Deepfake detection in voice biometrics is a classifier that runs alongside speaker verification and scores whether the incoming audio was generated synthetically, replayed from a recording, or spoken live. Speaker verification answers "is this the right person". Deepfake detection answers "is this a real person at all". Production systems need both, because a cloned voice can pass a verification check that has no liveness or synthesis test behind it.
Gnani Biometrics
runs passive verification and anti-spoof scoring on the same call audio, extracting 300+ voice features per call, and Gnani AI reports a 99%+ fraud detection rate and identity verification in under 5 seconds.
### What deepfake detection actually looks for
A speaker verification model compares an incoming sample against an enrolled voiceprint and returns a similarity score. That model was never trained to care where the audio came from. Deepfake detection is a separate decision trained on the artefacts that generation leaves behind.
#### Spectral artefacts
Neural vocoders reconstruct a waveform from an intermediate representation. That reconstruction is close enough to fool a listener and still leaves measurable structure in the high frequency bands, in harmonic spacing, and in the way energy decays at the end of voiced segments. Detection models learn those signatures rather than the content of the speech.
#### Prosody and timing
Human speech carries breath. Pauses land where the speaker runs out of air or thinks, not where a punctuation token sits. Phoneme transitions vary with fatigue, emotion and effort. Synthetic speech tends to be more regular than a person is, and that regularity is a signal.
#### Channel and environment
A live call picks up the room, the handset, the codec and the network. A replayed recording carries two channels stacked on top of each other, the original capture and the playback device. Liveness checks look for that double signature, along with micro echoes and ambient patterns that a clean synthetic file does not have.
#### Cross-lingual behaviour
Detection that keys on language content breaks the moment a caller code-switches, which in Indian contact centres is most of the time. Models built on the physical characteristics of speech production hold up across languages and accents. That matters when the same queue handles Hindi, Tamil and Hinglish inside a single shift. The
Gnani AI model stack
is trained on telephonic audio rather than studio recordings, which is the audio profile these systems meet in production.

### The four attack types and what catches each one
Teams often treat spoofing as one problem. It is four, and they fail in different ways. Buying a detection product without knowing which of the four your fraud pattern looks like is how deployments disappoint.
Attack type
How it is carried out
Signal that catches it
What it defeats on its own
Replay
A genuine recording of the customer is played down the line from a phone or speaker.
Liveness: double channel signature, micro echoes, room acoustics stacked on playback acoustics.
Speaker verification with no liveness layer.
Synthetic clone
A TTS or voice cloning model generates new speech from a short sample of the customer's voice.

Mimicry
A human impersonates the customer, sometimes with knowledge of their security answers.
Speaker verification itself, since the physical vocal tract differs even when the imitation sounds close.

Injection
Generated audio is fed straight into the call stream, bypassing the microphone and the room entirely.

Four spoofing attack types and the detection signal that catches each. Source: Gnani AI.
The practical consequence is that a single threshold does not serve all four. A replay attack and a zero-shot clone produce different score distributions, and tuning one down raises false accepts on the other. Ask any vendor for per-attack-type results rather than a single headline accuracy number.
### Where deepfake detection sits in an authentication flow
Detection is worth little if it fires after the money has moved. The useful position is early, passive, and continuous.
#### Passive enrolment and verification
Active verification asks the caller to repeat a passphrase. It works, and it costs the caller time and the agent patience. Passive verification builds the voiceprint from natural conversation, so the check happens while the caller explains why they rang. Gnani AI reports that removing security questions from the front of a call cuts 40 seconds from average handle time.
#### Scoring on every turn, not once
A single check at the start of a call leaves the rest of the conversation unprotected against a handover, where a legitimate caller is replaced after authentication. Continuous scoring across the call closes that gap and produces an audit trail that a compliance team can actually review.
#### Risk-tiered thresholds
A balance enquiry and a beneficiary change do not deserve the same threshold. Tiering by transaction risk lets you keep friction low on routine calls and raise the bar where loss exposure is real. Pair the biometric score with device, carrier and behavioural signals so an attacker has to defeat several independent checks at once. This is the pattern
is built around, alongside
Gnani Assist
for the agent-facing side of the same call.
### What to test before you sign
Vendor accuracy figures are measured on the vendor's own evaluation set. That set is rarely your traffic. A short structured pilot tells you more than a datasheet.
Run detection against your own recorded calls, at your own sample rate. A model evaluated on clean 16kHz audio behaves differently on 8kHz telephony.
Generate clones of consenting internal volunteers using the tools your attackers would actually reach for, and measure the detection rate per tool.
Measure false rejects on your hardest legitimate cases: callers with colds, elderly speakers, noisy streets, poor handsets.
Test code-switched calls specifically, alongside monolingual ones.
Ask for the score distribution rather than the pass or fail alone, so your risk team can set thresholds instead of inheriting them.
Confirm how long raw audio is retained and where the voiceprints live.
### Compliance and data handling
A voiceprint is not a password. Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, voiceprints and speaker embeddings are sensitive personal data, and the consent, retention and residency obligations that follow are stricter than those for a call recording. For a bank, RBI expectations on customer authentication apply on top. For an insurer, IRDAI. For a US healthcare deployment, HIPAA.
Three questions decide most of it. Where is the voiceprint stored. Who can export it. What happens to it when the customer withdraws consent. Deepfake detection stops being a research topic the first time a cloned voice clears your authentication flow. The build order that works is unglamorous: establish a baseline on your own recorded traffic, add passive verification so enrolment costs the customer nothing, layer anti-spoof and liveness scoring on top, then tier your thresholds by transaction risk instead of running one number for every call. ### Frequently asked questions
What is deepfake detection in voice biometrics?
Deepfake detection is a model that scores whether incoming call audio was spoken live by a person or produced synthetically. It runs alongside speaker verification rather than replacing it. Verification confirms identity against an enrolled voiceprint, and detection confirms the audio is genuine, which is what stops a cloned voice from passing a verification check.
Can voice biometrics detect AI-generated voices?
Yes, when an anti-spoof layer is present. Speaker verification on its own compares similarity and has no view on whether the sample was generated. Systems that add synthesis and liveness scoring catch cloned audio by the artefacts that generation leaves in the spectrum, the prosody and the channel. Detection quality varies by attack type, so ask for results broken out by clone, replay, mimicry and injection rather than one blended figure.
How is deepfake detection different from liveness detection?
Liveness detection asks whether the audio came from a live acoustic environment or from a playback device, which catches replay attacks. Deepfake detection asks whether the speech was generated by a model at all, which catches synthesis fed straight into the call. Most production deployments run both, because a high quality clone played through a speaker looks different from the same clone injected into the audio stream.
Does deepfake detection work across Indian languages?
Detection that relies on the physical characteristics of speech production, rather than on what is being said, is language independent in principle. In practice, the training audio matters. A model trained on clean English studio recordings will see more false rejects on 8kHz Hindi telephony with background noise. Test on your own language mix, including code-switched calls, before setting thresholds.
What accuracy should I expect from deepfake detection?
Expect the number to move with your audio. Detection performance depends on sample rate, codec, noise, call length and which generation tool produced the attack, so a single headline figure travels badly between deployments. Gnani AI reports a 99%+ fraud detection rate for Gnani Biometrics, measured on its own production traffic. Run your own evaluation on your own calls and treat any vendor figure, including that one, as a starting point.
How long does voice verification take on a live call?
Passive verification completes inside the first few seconds of natural conversation. Gnani AI reports identity verification in under 5 seconds and a 40 second reduction in average handle time from removing security questions. The caller does not repeat a passphrase, so the saving comes out of the agent's time rather than the customer's patience.

### Voice biometric authentication in AI agents, in short
Voice biometric authentication lets an AI voice agent confirm who is speaking from the sound of their voice, without asking for a date of birth, a mother's maiden name or the last four digits of an account. Inside an agent, it runs as a scoring service alongside speech recognition: the agent keeps talking, a speaker model scores the audio against an enrolled template, and a policy decides what the caller is allowed to do next. The score is an input to that policy, never the decision itself. A deployment is only as good as the layers around the score: liveness, replay detection, channel analysis and a step-up rule for high-risk actions.
### What voice biometric authentication actually does inside an agent
Two different things happen to the same audio stream, and confusing them causes most of the design mistakes in this area. Speech recognition turns the audio into words so the agent can understand intent. Speaker recognition ignores the words and measures the voice itself: pitch, formant structure, speaking rate, glottal characteristics, the geometry of the vocal tract. Gnani AI reports that
Gnani Biometrics
extracts more than 300 voice features per call and holds them as a mathematical template rather than as stored audio.
That distinction matters for the architecture. Transcription is a per-turn job, and
Gnani Prisma v2.5
handles it as a stream. Verification is a per-caller job that can resolve once and then inform every turn after it. In an agent that runs across voice, WhatsApp, chat and SMS, only the voice channel produces a voiceprint at all, so the identity decision has to be expressed in a way the rest of the workflow can act on.
#### A template is not a recording
An enrolled voiceprint is a set of numbers derived from speech. It cannot be played back, and it does not reconstruct the original audio. That is a real structural advantage over a password database, because a leaked template does not hand an attacker a working credential the way a leaked password hash eventually can. It is also the source of the technology's hardest constraint: a caller whose template is compromised cannot be issued a new voice. Treat a voiceprint as a durable identifier, not a rotatable secret.

### Where verification sits in the agent turn loop
An AI voice agent has a tight cycle: capture audio, transcribe, decide, speak. Verification has to fit inside that cycle without adding a pause the caller can hear. There are two patterns, and most enterprise deployments use both.
#### Passive verification
The speaker model scores whatever the caller says naturally while the agent handles the opening of the call. Nobody is asked to repeat a phrase. By the time the caller states what they want, a score already exists. Gnani AI reports sub-second passive verification on its own platform and identity confirmed in under five seconds end to end. Passive verification is what removes the security-question script from the front of the call, and it is the pattern that produces the handle-time saving. Gnani AI reports a 40 second reduction in average handle time across its biometrics deployments.
#### Active verification
The agent asks for a fixed passphrase. This gives the model clean, predictable audio and a clear consent moment, which is useful at enrolment and at step-up. It costs a turn, so it belongs at the points where the extra friction is proportionate: first enrolment, a high-value transfer, a payee change. Using it as the default opening puts the security question back in a different costume.
### The latency budget for voice biometric authentication
Verification competes for the same milliseconds as everything else in the turn. Gnani AI reports response latency under 800ms in live conversations on
Gnani Agents
, and sub-200ms streaming from
Prisma v2.5
. A scoring call that blocks the agent's reply will be felt by the caller even if the number looks small on a dashboard.
The design that holds up is asynchronous. Scoring runs on a parallel path and writes a confidence value into the session state. The agent reads that value when it needs to, which is at the moment the caller asks for something the policy protects, not at hello. Anything that can be answered without identity, such as a branch timing or a policy question, never waits on the score at all.
### What a match does not prove
A high similarity score says the audio is acoustically consistent with the enrolled template. It does not say a person is present, that the speech was produced by a human larynx rather than a model, that the audio was captured now rather than last week, or that the device and route are the ones you expect. Each of those is a separate control, and each has its own failure mode. A synthetic clone built from a short sample of a target's public speech can score well against an acoustic-only system, and that class of attack gets cheaper as speech synthesis improves.
This is why the honest framing for buyers is that voice biometric authentication raises the cost of an attack rather than ending it. Any vendor, including Gnani AI, that presents a single score as proof of identity is describing a demo and not a production control.

### Handling a low score without breaking the call
The interesting engineering is not the pass path. It is what the agent does when the score lands in the middle. A binary gate at a fixed threshold produces the worst of both outcomes: genuine callers with a cold, a noisy line or an unusual handset get rejected, and a decent clone at the same threshold gets through.
Risk-based scoring works better. The agent combines the voice score with what the caller is trying to do. A balance enquiry clears on a moderate score. A payee change or a large transfer requires a second factor regardless of how confident the voice model is. When confidence is marginal, the fallback has to be genuinely different from the voiceprint, not the security-question script the deployment was meant to retire. Falling back to knowledge-based questions restores the exact weakness the project set out to remove.
The handoff matters too. When the agent escalates, the human should receive the conversation history and the identity state together. Gnani AI reports context-aware handoff with full conversation history on Gnani Agents, and real-time guidance for the receiving human through

### Voiceprints are sensitive biometric data
Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, a voiceprint is biometric personal data. Under GDPR it is special category data. Speaker embeddings sit in the highest sensitivity tier that exists in most enterprise data classifications, and they should be handled that way from the first day of a pilot.

Vendor accuracy numbers are measured on the vendor's audio. Yours is 8kHz telephony with your accents, your languages and your line quality. Ask for five things.
False accept and false reject curves on your own recordings, at your own sample rate, across the full operating range rather than a single flattering point.
A live clone test. Supply thirty seconds of a consenting colleague's voice, let the vendor build a current-generation clone, and watch what the system scores.

### Where this leaves you
Voice biometric authentication earns its place in an AI agent by removing a slow, unreliable interrogation from the front of every call and replacing it with a signal the agent can act on in under a second. It earns trust by being treated as one input to a policy that also knows what the caller is trying to do. Build the low-confidence path and the step-up rule before you tune the threshold, test the system against a clone of a voice you control, and keep the template handling under the same scrutiny as any other biometric store. If you want to see the verification path running inside a live agent,
book a demo
, or read how the pieces fit together across
the enterprise product line
.
### Frequently asked questions
What is voice biometric authentication in an AI agent?
It is speaker verification running alongside the agent's speech recognition, scoring the caller's voice against an enrolled template and passing a confidence value to the agent's policy. The agent then decides what the caller may do based on that value and the risk of the requested action.
Is voice biometric authentication secure enough for banking?
It is secure enough as one factor inside a risk-based policy, and not secure enough as the only gate in front of money movement. It removes the phishing and guessing attacks that knowledge-based questions suffer from, and it introduces a cloning attack surface that liveness, replay detection and a second factor on high-value actions are there to answer.
Can a cloned voice defeat voice biometric authentication?
A good clone can defeat a system that scores acoustic similarity alone. It has a much harder time against a system that also checks liveness, replay artefacts, channel and device signals, and behaviour during the call, and that requires a second factor before a high-risk action completes.
How long does voice enrolment take?
Enrolment needs enough clean speech for the model to build a stable template, which is usually captured either during a short active passphrase step or passively across an ordinary conversation. The practical question for a deployment is not the length of a single enrolment but how you enrol a large existing customer base without a campaign nobody answers.
Does voice biometric authentication work across Indian languages?
Speaker recognition measures voice characteristics rather than words, so a template built in one language generally scores against speech in another. Gnani AI lists cross-lingual enrolment as a capability of Gnani Biometrics. Code-mixed speech is worth testing specifically, because the surrounding recognition and agent layers behave differently on it even when the speaker model does not.
Is voiceprint data personally identifiable information?
Yes, and at the top of the sensitivity scale. A voiceprint is biometric personal data under the DPDP Act and special category data under GDPR, which means explicit consent, defined retention, encryption, least-privilege access and audit logging are baseline requirements rather than hardening steps.

### TL;DR
Voice authentication verifies a caller from the acoustic and behavioural characteristics of their speech rather than from something they know. A bank enrols a customer once, builds a voiceprint from that audio, and compares every later call against it. Done passively, the check runs in the background of normal conversation and finishes in under five seconds, which removes the security-question ritual that drags out contact centre calls.
Gnani Biometrics

### What voice authentication is, and why banks are moving to it
Knowledge-based authentication asks the caller to prove identity with a PIN, a password, a one-time code or a set of challenge questions. Every one of those can be phished, shoulder-surfed, socially engineered or simply forgotten. The burden sits on the customer to keep a secret, and the bank inherits the failure when they don't.
Voice authentication moves the proof from something the caller knows to something the caller is. The system analyses physical characteristics of the vocal tract and learned characteristics of how a person speaks, then derives a mathematical template. That template is the voiceprint. It is not a recording and it cannot be played back as audio.
For a bank, the appeal is operational as much as it is security. Fingerprint and iris scanning both need a sensor in the customer's hands. Voice needs a phone line, which the customer is already on. That makes voice the only biometric that works natively on the inbound call channel, where most authentication friction actually sits. Gnani AI reports that passive verification with
cuts roughly 40 seconds from average handle time.
#### Text-dependent and text-independent verification
Text-dependent systems ask the caller to speak a fixed passphrase. Enrolment is quick because the system knows exactly what it will hear, and matching is straightforward. The weakness is that a fixed phrase is a fixed target. Anyone who captures a recording of it has captured the credential.
Text-independent systems verify from whatever the caller happens to say. Enrolment takes longer and the matching problem is harder, but the credential cannot be replayed because there is nothing fixed to replay. For Indian contact centres there is a second argument: a text-independent model that handles cross-lingual enrolment can verify a customer who enrolled in Hindi and later calls speaking Tamil.

Customer experience
Customer is aware of a security step and can fail it.
Invisible to the customer. Nothing to remember or get wrong.
Language handling
Tied to the language the passphrase was enrolled in.
Cross-lingual enrolment lets a customer enrol in one language and verify in another.
Best fit
Low-volume, high-assurance flows where an explicit step is acceptable.
High-volume inbound contact centre traffic where handle time matters.
Passive verification is the stronger pattern for banking. It verifies continuously rather than once at the top of the call, so an attacker who hands the phone over after authentication gets caught. It also removes the only part of the interaction the customer experiences as a security step, which is where most of the drop-off happens.
### How a voice authentication check actually runs
Enrolment comes first. The system captures speech, either from a dedicated enrolment call or from ordinary conversation, and extracts features across multiple frequency bands. Those features become a template stored against the customer record.
On every later call, the same extraction runs against the live audio and the result is scored against the stored template. The score is a probability, not a yes or no, and the bank sets the threshold. A high threshold rejects more genuine customers. A low one admits more impostors. Where that line sits is a risk decision, not a technical one, and it should differ between a balance enquiry and a funds transfer.
Telephony audio is the hard part. Call audio arrives at 8kHz, compressed, often with background noise and frequently code-mixed across two languages mid-sentence. A model trained on clean studio recordings degrades badly here.
Gnani Prisma v2.5
is trained on 14M+ hours of real telephonic audio and reports under 4% word error rate on Indian speech, which is the kind of baseline the authentication layer needs underneath it.
### Where voice authentication earns its place in a bank
#### Contact centre authentication
This is the clearest case. Security questions consume the opening minutes of a call, fail often, and annoy the customer who gets them wrong. Passive verification completes while the agent is still greeting the caller. Gnani AI reports verification in under five seconds and a 20%+ improvement in customer satisfaction attributable to faster verification.
#### Fraud and deepfake detection
Synthetic speech is now cheap and good. Any voice authentication deployment that treats a voice match as sufficient proof is building on sand, and the serious systems have moved to detecting whether the audio is genuine at all. Gnani AI reports a 99%+ fraud detection rate for
, which combines speaker matching with anti-spoof and deepfake checks on the same stream. Ask any vendor to demonstrate both, separately, on your own audio.
#### KYC and financial inclusion
Language-independent verification matters in markets where customers do not share a language with the contact centre. A customer who cannot complete an app-based check, or who cannot read the screen, can still complete a voice check. Paired with
voice agents that handle onboarding flows
, this opens remote servicing to customers that branch and app journeys miss.
### What voice authentication does not solve
It is worth being direct about the limits, because the category oversells itself.
Voice authentication does not survive on its own. A sufficiently good clone, built from audio the customer has published themselves, will eventually defeat speaker matching. The defence is the liveness and spoof layer, and that layer is adversarial, which means it needs updating as attacks improve. A vendor who does not talk about retraining cadence is not thinking about this properly.
Enrolment coverage is the other practical limit. A voiceprint only helps for customers who have one, and enrolment rates in real deployments climb slowly. Plan for a long period where the majority of callers still need a fallback path, and make that fallback good rather than punitive.
Illness, poor line quality and ambient noise all degrade match confidence. The honest answer is a graceful step-down to a second factor, not a hard rejection.
### Regulatory ground to cover before deployment
Voiceprints and speaker embeddings are biometric data, and in India they sit under the DPDP Act with the handling obligations that implies: a lawful basis for collection, a stated purpose, retention limits and a deletion path the customer can actually use. Banks also answer to RBI expectations on authentication and customer data, and outbound calling brings TRAI consent and DND rules into scope.
Three questions decide most deployments. Where does the voiceprint live. Who can read it. What happens to it when the customer closes the account. A deployment model that keeps the templates inside the bank's own network answers all three more cleanly than one that does not, which is the argument for running the stack on infrastructure the bank controls.
Artha
is Gnani AI's sovereign deployment of its models for exactly this case, running on-premise or in a private cloud.
None of this is legal advice, and regulatory positions move. Confirm with your legal and compliance team before deployment.
### How to evaluate a voice authentication vendor
Test on your own call audio, not on a demo recording. The gap between a vendor's clean-audio numbers and your 8kHz production traffic is where most pilots fail.
Ask for false accept and false reject rates at a stated threshold, on telephony audio, in the languages your customers actually use. A single accuracy percentage with no threshold attached tells you nothing. Ask separately about deepfake detection, because speaker matching and spoof detection are different problems and some vendors ship only the first.
Then ask the unglamorous questions. How long does enrolment take. What is the fallback when a match fails. Which telephony platforms are supported natively, and which need integration work. Gnani AI publishes integrations with Avaya, Cisco, Five9 and core banking systems, which is the kind of list worth checking against your own stack. Gnani AI does not publish pricing, so commercial terms come through the sales conversation, which is a genuine disadvantage if you are trying to compare options quickly.
On certifications, Gnani AI is SOC 2 Type 2 certified and ISO 27001 certified, and HIPAA, GDPR and PCI-DSS compliant. Ask every vendor for scope and expiry dates rather than accepting a logo on a page.
### Getting voice authentication into production
Voice authentication is the rare security control that makes the customer experience better rather than worse, which is why it has moved from pilot to production across banking so quickly. The deployments that work treat it as one layer in a stack: passive verification for speed, spoof detection for the attacks that matter, and a well-designed fallback for the calls where confidence is low. Gnani AI runs 30M+ daily voice interactions across 200+ enterprise deployments, with cloud, private cloud, on-premise and air-gapped options. If you want to see voice authentication running on your own call audio,
book a demo
.
### Frequently asked questions
What is voice authentication in banking?
Voice authentication in banking verifies a customer's identity from the characteristics of their speech instead of from a PIN, password or security question. The bank enrols the customer once, stores a mathematical voiceprint derived from that audio, and compares later calls against it. It is used mainly on inbound contact centre calls, where it replaces the knowledge-based questions that slow the call down.
How secure is voice authentication compared to a password?
Voice authentication is harder to phish than a password, because there is no secret the customer can be tricked into revealing. It is not unbreakable. Synthetic speech can imitate a voice convincingly, so a deployment needs anti-spoof and deepfake detection alongside speaker matching, and it works best as one factor among several rather than on its own.
What is the difference between active and passive voice authentication?
Active voice authentication asks the caller to speak a set passphrase. Passive voice authentication verifies from ordinary conversation with no special step. Passive is generally preferred in banking because it verifies continuously through the call rather than once at the start, and because it removes the friction the customer notices.
Can voice authentication detect AI-generated or cloned voices?
Systems built for this can. Detection is a separate capability from speaker matching, and it works by looking for artefacts of synthesis in the audio rather than by comparing the voice to a template. Gnani AI reports a 99%+ fraud detection rate for Gnani Biometrics, which runs both checks on the same stream. Ask any vendor to demonstrate spoof detection separately from voice matching.
Is voice data covered by the DPDP Act?
Voiceprints and speaker embeddings are biometric data and fall under the DPDP Act in India, which means collection needs a lawful basis and a stated purpose, and customers need a workable route to deletion. Banks should also work through RBI expectations on authentication and, for outbound calling, TRAI consent and DND rules. Confirm with your legal and compliance team before deployment.
How long does voice enrolment take?
It depends on the method. Text-dependent enrolment asks the customer to repeat a passphrase several times and takes under a minute. Text-independent enrolment builds the voiceprint from ordinary conversation, so it adds nothing to the call, but it needs enough speech across one or more calls before the template is usable.

### TL;DR
Voice recognition security in banking means verifying who is speaking, not what they said. The bank enrols a customer once, stores a mathematical voiceprint rather than a recording, and compares every later call against it. It removes the knowledge questions that attackers can research or phish, and it cuts verification from a scripted interrogation to a few seconds of ordinary conversation. It does not, on its own, prove that a live human is on the line. Synthetic speech is now good enough that the acoustic match has to sit inside a layered control set: liveness detection, replay and injection detection, channel signals, and risk-based step-up on the actions that actually move money.
### What voice recognition security actually checks
Two different things get called voice recognition. One is transcription, which turns speech into text and cares only about the words. The other is speaker recognition, which ignores the words and measures the speaker. Banking security uses the second.
An enrolment sample is converted into a voiceprint: a numeric template describing how a particular vocal tract produces sound.
Gnani Biometrics
derives more than 300 voice features per call for that template. The template is not audio. It cannot be played back, and on its own it is not intelligible, which is why it is stored and compared rather than the recording.
That distinction matters operationally. A transcription engine such as
Prisma v2.5
, trained on more than 14 million hours of real telephonic audio, is what lets the same call also be understood, routed and analysed. Speaker verification runs alongside it on the same stream. Banks that treat the two as one product tend to discover the gap during procurement.
ENTERPRISE VOICE AI

200+ Enterprises · 30M daily calls · 10 Indic languages

### Why banks moved off knowledge-based verification
Knowledge-based authentication asks for things a customer knows. Date of birth, last transaction, mother's maiden name, a one-time passcode read aloud. Each of those can be researched, bought, socially engineered or intercepted, and every one of them costs call time before the conversation starts.
Voice changes the economics on both sides. The credential is not transferable in the way a passcode is, and the check happens while the customer is already talking. Gnani AI reports sub-second scoring with identity confirmed in under five seconds, a 99% or better fraud detection rate, and around 40 seconds removed from average handle time across its
enterprise voice platform
deployments. Those are vendor figures measured under Gnani AI's own conditions, so treat them as a starting point for your own test rather than a benchmark.
The weakness is the mirror image of the strength. A password can be reset. A voice cannot. If a template store is breached, the remediation is re-enrolment under a new feature extractor, not a password reset email.
### Active, passive and hybrid verification compared
Banks deploy voice recognition security in three shapes. The choice is not really about accuracy. It is about where the friction lands and which regulator is looking.
Voice verification models in banking
Dimension
Active
Passive
Hybrid
What the customer does
Repeats an enrolled passphrase on request

Nothing by default. Repeats a phrase only when risk rises

Balance and statement enquiries, status checks, high call volume IVR
Mixed contact centre traffic where a minority of calls move money
Main weakness
Announces the check, which tells an attacker what to prepare for
A silent check is easy to under-disclose, which is a compliance risk
Two paths to test, tune and audit instead of one
#### Active verification
The customer repeats an enrolled phrase. Enrolment is explicit, consent is easy to evidence, and the audio the system compares is short and controlled. It also announces itself, which is useful for high-risk actions and irritating for a balance enquiry.
#### Passive verification
The system scores the customer's normal speech during the first few seconds of the call. Nothing is repeated and nothing is announced mid-conversation, so handle time drops. The consent and disclosure burden moves to enrolment and to the call opening, where it has to be handled properly rather than quietly.
#### Hybrid
Passive scoring carries the routine traffic. An active challenge fires only when the score is low, the channel looks wrong, or the customer asks for something that changes money or contact details. Most banks that run voice at scale end up here, because it puts the friction on the small share of calls that deserve it.
### What a voiceprint match does not prove
A high match score says the acoustic pattern resembles the enrolled speaker. It says nothing about four other things a fraud team cares about.
Liveness.
Whether a person is speaking now, or a model is generating speech that sounds like them.
Recency.
Whether the audio was captured in this call or replayed from an earlier one.
Injection path.
Whether the audio arrived through a handset and a carrier, or was fed straight into the session by a virtual device.
Intent.
Whether the genuine customer is speaking freely or being coached through the call by someone else.
The threat is not theoretical. In a Gartner survey of 302 cybersecurity leaders published in September 2025, 43% reported at least one deepfake incident on an audio call. Voice cloning quality has kept improving since, which is why the acoustic layer has to be treated as one signal among several rather than the decision itself.
### The layers that decide whether a clone gets through
#### Liveness and anti-spoof detection
Anti-spoof models look for the artefacts that synthesis leaves behind: unnatural breath placement, micro-timing that is too regular, spectral detail that does not match a physical vocal tract.
ships anti-spoof and deepfake detection alongside the matcher for this reason. Ask any vendor when their spoof model was last retrained, because this is the layer that ages fastest.
#### Replay and injection detection
Replay detection is the most mature control in the set. Recorded-then-replayed audio carries a second acoustic path, and that is detectable. Injection is harder and increasingly more common, because a virtual audio device bypasses the microphone entirely.
#### Channel and device signals
Codec, jitter, carrier route and device fingerprint are cheap signals that a pure acoustic matcher ignores. A voiceprint that matches perfectly but arrives over an unexpected route on a device first seen ten minutes ago is a different risk from the same match on the handset the customer has used for three years.
#### Risk-based step-up
The score should feed a policy, not a gate. A balance enquiry can clear on a moderate score. A payee change, a limit increase or a transfer above a threshold should demand more, whether that is an active phrase, an in-app confirmation or a callback. This is also where
Gnani Analytics
earns its place, because the audit trail of which score allowed which action is what a regulator will ask for.
### Voiceprints are biometric personal data
Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, a voiceprint is personal data, and most banking counsel treat it as sensitive. The GDPR classifies biometric data used for unique identification as a special category. Both regimes push in the same direction: explicit and specific consent at enrolment, a defined retention period, encryption at rest and in transit, least-privilege access to the template store, and an audit log of every read.
On top of that, RBI expectations apply to the banking deployment, TRAI rules apply to outbound calling and consent, and HIPAA applies if the same platform touches US health data. Voice agents also have to disclose that they are AI in the scripts and enrolment flows they run. Gnani AI publishes SOC 2 Type 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, GDPR and PCI-DSS, and supports cloud, private cloud, on-premise and air-gapped deployment through
Artha
for banks that cannot send voice data off their own infrastructure. None of this is legal advice. Confirm the applicable obligations with your legal and compliance team before a production decision.
### How to test a voice recognition security vendor
Vendor accuracy numbers, including Gnani AI's, are measured on the vendor's data under the vendor's conditions. Run these five tests on yours.
Ask for the full error curve, not one operating point.
A single false-accept rate hides the trade-off. You want false accept against false reject across the whole threshold range, measured on your own 8 kHz telephony audio.
Commission a live clone attempt.
Give a red team 30 seconds of a consenting employee's voice and current tooling, then run it at the matcher through a real call path.
Test replay and injection separately.
A vendor strong on replay can still be weak on a virtual audio device, and the two failures look identical in a summary report.
Watch the low-confidence path.
What the system does when it is unsure matters more than what it does when it is certain. Confirm the fallback is a step-up, not a silent pass.
Inspect template storage.
Encryption, key custody, access control, retention, deletion on request, and whether templates can be exported if you change vendor.
### Where this leaves a banking security team
Voice recognition security in banking is worth deploying, and it is not a control you can deploy alone. It removes a class of attack that knowledge-based verification invites, it gives back call time that customers notice, and it hands fraud teams a signal they did not previously have. It also introduces an irrevocable credential and a synthetic-speech attack surface that did not exist five years ago. The banks that get value from it are the ones that treat the voiceprint as one input to a risk decision, keep the spoof models current, and test the whole path rather than the matcher.
If you are scoping a deployment, the
BFSI solutions overview
covers the workflows this usually sits inside, and the
model pages
list the recognition and synthesis layers it runs on. For the broader question of whether voice biometrics can be spoofed at all, see
our analysis of voice biometric safety and spoofing
, and for the case against passwords specifically,
why banks are replacing passwords with voice
.
### Frequently asked questions
Can voice AI handle account verification in a bank?
Yes, for the identification step. A passive or active voiceprint check can confirm the caller matches the enrolled customer within the first seconds of a call, which is enough to release account information under most banks' policies. Money movement should require an additional factor, because the voiceprint confirms identity, not liveness or intent.
How accurate is voice biometrics?
Accuracy depends entirely on your audio, not on a headline number. Published rates come from vendor test sets recorded under favourable conditions. On 8 kHz telephony audio with background noise, code-switching and low-cost handsets, the same system performs differently. Ask for the full false accept and false reject curve and reproduce it on your own call recordings before committing to a threshold.
Why do banks need voice security when they already have OTP?
One-time passcodes protect the channel, not the caller. They can be intercepted through SIM swap, read out to a social engineer, or approved by a customer who has been talked into it. A voiceprint is checked passively against the person speaking, so it covers a failure mode that OTP does not. Most banks run both rather than replacing one with the other.
Is voice authentication safe for banks given deepfakes?
It is safe when it is layered and unsafe when it is the only check. Synthetic speech can defeat an acoustic matcher on its own. It has to get past liveness detection, replay and injection detection, channel analysis and a step-up policy as well, and that combination is still a materially harder target than a date of birth and a passcode.
What is the difference between active and passive voice biometrics?
Active verification asks the customer to repeat an enrolled phrase. Passive verification scores their normal speech during the conversation without interrupting it. Active is easier to evidence for consent and better suited to high-risk actions. Passive is faster and invisible. Hybrid deployments use passive by default and escalate to active on risk.
How long does voice biometric enrolment take?
Active enrolment takes one short phrase repeated a few times, usually inside a single call. Passive enrolment can be built from existing consented call audio, which means a bank with call recordings can enrol a large part of its base without contacting customers, provided the original consent and the retention policy cover that use. Confirm that second point with your compliance team before planning a bulk enrolment.

### Voice biometrics, the short answer
TL;DR:
Voice biometrics is the identification or verification of a person from the characteristics of their voice. The system builds a mathematical representation of how someone speaks, called a voiceprint, and compares later speech against it. It is used mainly to replace knowledge-based authentication in contact centres, where security questions are slow, easy to socially engineer and frustrating for the caller. Modern deployments run passively in the background of a normal conversation and pair identification with anti-spoofing, because synthetic speech has made liveness detection as important as the match itself.
### What voice biometrics means
A voiceprint is not a recording. It is a vector derived from measurable properties of speech, and it cannot be played back as audio. That distinction matters legally as well as technically, because a voiceprint is biometric data in its own right and carries obligations a call recording does not.
#### Physiological and behavioural features
Two families of signal go into the representation.
Physiological features
come from the shape of the vocal tract, nasal cavity and larynx. They are stable and hard to imitate deliberately.
Behavioural features
cover rhythm, pace, stress patterns and pronunciation habits. They carry useful signal but drift with illness, fatigue and age.
Gnani Biometrics
extracts more than 300 voice features per call across both families, and supports cross-lingual enrolment so a customer enrolled speaking one language still verifies when they call back in another.
#### Active against passive enrolment
Active enrolment asks the caller to repeat a set phrase. It is explicit and easy to consent to, but it adds a step and the phrase can be captured. Passive enrolment builds the voiceprint from natural conversation during a normal call, so there is nothing to remember and nothing to steal, though the consent flow has to be designed deliberately rather than inferred.
### How voice biometrics works in a live call
Four stages run in sequence, usually inside the first few seconds of speech.
Capture and conditioning.
Audio arrives, often as 8kHz telephony with line noise, and is segmented to isolate the speaker.
Feature extraction.
The acoustic properties are reduced to a vector. Nothing intelligible is retained at this stage.
Comparison and scoring.
The vector is matched against the enrolled voiceprint and a confidence score is produced, with a threshold set by the business against its own tolerance for false accepts and false rejects.
Liveness and spoof detection.
The audio is checked for signs of replay, synthesis or conversion before the score is trusted.
Gnani AI reports a fraud detection rate above 99%, identity verification in under 5 seconds, a 40 second reduction in average handle time and more than 20% improvement in customer satisfaction from faster verification. The quality of stage one decides the rest, which is why the speech layer matters:
Gnani Prisma v2.5

### Where voice biometrics is used by industry

and

### Deepfakes and the anti-spoofing question
Synthetic speech is now good enough that a match score on its own is not evidence of a live human. A deployment that verifies identity without checking liveness has moved the attack surface rather than closed it. Anti-spoofing looks for the artefacts that separate generated or replayed audio from a live vocal tract, and it has to be treated as a first-class part of the system rather than an option.
Gnani Biometrics includes anti-spoof and deepfake detection alongside verification for this reason. The practical control for a security team is to treat the spoof check and the match score as two independent gates, and to log both so an audit can reconstruct why a caller was admitted.
Gnani Analytics

### Compliance: voiceprints are sensitive biometric data
A voiceprint is biometric data and carries the highest sensitivity classification. Under the DPDP Act, Indian customer data of this kind needs a lawful basis, informed consent, stated retention limits and defensible deletion. BFSI deployments attract RBI guidance, insurance attracts IRDAI, healthcare in the United States attracts HIPAA, and European data attracts GDPR, which treats biometric data used for identification as a special category.
Four controls belong in the design: explicit consent captured before enrolment rather than inferred from continued use, encryption of voiceprints in transit and at rest with least-privilege access, a retention and deletion policy agreed with the business, and audit logging of every match and every spoof check. Gnani AI is SOC 2 Type 2 certified, ISO 27001 certified, and HIPAA, GDPR and PCI-DSS compliant, and the stack deploys in cloud, private cloud, on-premise or air-gapped environments, so voiceprints need never leave the customer environment. ### Voice biometrics earns its place at the start of the call
The case for voice biometrics is not that it is a novel way to log in. It is that the first ninety seconds of a contact centre call are currently spent on questions that are slow for the customer and weak against a determined attacker. What is the difference between active and passive voice biometrics?
Active verification asks the caller to repeat a set phrase, which is explicit and easy to evidence but adds a step and can be replayed if captured. ### TL;DR
Voice authentication verifies who a caller is by comparing the live audio of their speech against a stored voiceprint, a mathematical model of how that person's vocal tract and speaking habits shape sound. It replaces the security questions an agent would otherwise ask, and it runs while the conversation is already underway, so the caller does not repeat a passphrase or wait for an OTP. The technology is mature enough for production use in banking and insurance contact centres. It is also imperfect: synthetic speech, poor line quality and a caller with a cold all degrade it, which is why voiceprints belong inside a layered identity check rather than alone at the front of one.
### What is voice authentication?
Voice authentication is biometric identity verification that uses the sound of a person's speech as the credential. Gnani AI groups it with fraud detection and anti-spoofing under
Gnani Biometrics
, the product line that handles caller identity inside a voice channel.
The system extracts features from an audio sample and stores them as a voiceprint. A voiceprint is not a recording. It is a vector derived from physical traits such as vocal tract length, nasal passage shape and glottal behaviour, combined with behavioural traits such as pace, stress placement and pronunciation. Two people can say the same sentence and produce very different vectors.
One naming point worth settling early, because the search results conflate them. Voice recognition authentication and speech recognition are different jobs. Speech recognition answers what was said, which is what an ASR model like
Prisma v2.5
does. Voice authentication answers who said it. A production stack usually runs both on the same audio, for different reasons.
### How voice authentication works
#### Enrolment
Enrolment captures a reference sample and turns it into the stored voiceprint. Text-dependent enrolment asks the caller to repeat a fixed phrase. Text-independent enrolment builds the voiceprint from whatever the caller happens to say, which usually means a longer capture window but a much better experience later.
The enrolment sample sets the ceiling for everything that follows. A voiceprint built from thirty seconds of clean audio behaves differently from one built from six seconds over a congested mobile line, and no amount of tuning at verification time recovers that.
#### Verification
At verification the system extracts the same features from live audio and scores the match against the stored voiceprint. The score is continuous, not binary, so deployment involves picking a threshold. Raise it and you reject more genuine customers. Lower it and you accept more impostors. That trade-off is the single most consequential configuration decision in a biometric voice authentication system, and it is the one most often left at a vendor default.
Gnani AI reports that its biometrics module extracts 300 or more voice features per call and verifies a caller in under five seconds, with a fraud detection rate above 99 percent, according to figures published on the
Gnani AI enterprise product page
. Those are vendor-stated numbers measured on Gnani AI's own traffic mix. Ask any vendor, this one included, for the false acceptance and false rejection rates at the specific threshold they propose for your deployment, because a headline detection rate without a stated operating point does not tell you what you need to know.
#### Active and passive modes
Active authentication interrupts the caller to collect a passphrase. Passive authentication listens to the natural conversation and scores continuously, so verification finishes while the caller is still explaining why they called. Passive is the better experience and the harder engineering problem, because it has to work on unconstrained speech across accents, code-switching and background noise.
Gnani AI reports a 40 second reduction in average handle time and a 20 percent or better improvement in customer satisfaction from faster verification. Both figures come from the same vendor page and reflect Gnani AI deployments rather than an independent study.
### Voice authentication compared with other biometric methods
Each modality fails differently. The useful comparison is not which one is most accurate in a lab, since that depends entirely on the test set, but which one fits the channel you actually operate in.
Method
