Agent assist is AI that supports a human agent during a live conversation. It transcribes the call as it happens, retrieves the matching policy or account answer, prompts the next best action, and generates the summary and CRM update afterwards. The agent stays in control of the conversation.
How is agent assist different from an AI voice agent?
An AI voice agent handles the call itself with no human on the line. Agent assist never speaks to the customer. It changes what the human agent knows and how quickly they know it, which is why the two are usually deployed together on different call types.
What does agent assist improve?
Gnani AI reports an 18% improvement in agent efficiency, 70% faster time to proficiency for new hires, a 30% increase in CSAT and a 90%+ reduction in after-call admin. First contact resolution and policy adherence are the harder metrics to move and the more honest ones to track.
Does agent assist work for Indian regional languages?
Yes, when the speech layer underneath is trained for it. Gnani Prisma v2.5 is trained on 14M+ hours of real telephonic audio, supports 10+ Indic languages in production, and reports 96% code-switching accuracy for mixed Hindi-English speech.
What should we check before buying agent assist?
Word error rate on 8kHz telephony audio in your own languages, end to end suggestion latency, how knowledge is ingested and updated, whether it runs inside your existing CRM, and which deployment modes are available for your regulatory position.
Is agent assist subject to data protection rules in India?
Call audio and transcripts are personal data under the DPDP Act, with RBI, IRDAI and TRAI obligations layered on by sector. Confirm with your legal and compliance team before deployment.

## What Is an AI Voice Agent? How It Works in Indian Languages and Where Enterprises Use It
November 17, 2026
•
5
mins read
Pratik Kumar
Product Marketing Lead
heading
Summarise with
GPT
CL
PPLX
Stay Updated
Get weekly update from Gnani AI
Thank You! Your submission has been received.
Oops! Something went wrong while submitting the form.
### TL;DR
What it is:
An AI voice agent is software that holds a natural phone conversation and gets the task done. It listens, understands, takes action in your systems and replies in a human-sounding voice.
How it works:
Each turn runs through speech recognition, a language model, API calls and text to speech. The whole loop needs to finish in about a second to feel natural.
Why India is harder:
Calls arrive as thin 8 kHz phone audio, people mix languages mid-sentence, and amounts and dates sound like "dhai hazaar" and "parso". Generic global models often miss these.
Where it works best:
High-volume, repeatable calls such as EMI reminders, early collections, lead qualification, renewals, KYC, delivery confirmations and tier-1 support.
Rules to follow:
TRAI's 1600 number series for financial service calls, RBI's 8 am to 7 pm window for recovery calls, and the DPDP Act and Rules for consent and data.
How to choose:
Test vendors on your own recorded calls and real mobile calls, check how they handle numbers and interruptions, and compare cost per resolved call, not per minute.
### What is an AI voice agent?
An AI voice agent is a conversational AI system that holds two-way spoken conversations and completes tasks, not just answers questions. Ask it to reschedule a delivery, and it checks the slot and books it. Tell it your card was blocked, and it verifies who you are, raises the request and tells you when it will be fixed.
Three things set an AI voice agent apart from older phone automation:
It understands open speech.
Callers say things however they like. "Mera card band ho gaya" and "my card is not working since morning" both lead to the same place.
It decides the next step.
A language model plans the conversation from
your policies and scenarios
and the caller's history. It does not just follow a fixed tree.
It acts.
Through APIs, it reads and writes to your systems, so the call ends with something done, not a ticket for someone else.
You will also see the terms "voice bot", "AI voice bot", "AI calling agent" and "conversational IVR". People use them loosely, so it helps to see where each one sits.
### AI voice agent vs voice bot vs IVR
An IVR makes callers press keys through a fixed menu. A voice bot (or AI voice bot) understands short spoken commands but follows a script. An AI voice agent holds an open conversation, handles interruptions and mixed languages, and completes the task end to end by working directly in your business systems.
Feature
Traditional IVR
Voice bot
AI voice agent
How callers interact
Press 1, press 2
Short spoken commands
Natural, open conversation
Languages
One recording per language
Usually one per flow
Many languages, including mixed speech in one call
Handles interruptions
No
Rarely
Yes, it stops and listens
Takes actions
Limited (balance, status)
Scripted lookups
Reads and writes to CRM, LOS, ticketing, payments
Changes in behavior

Edit the flow
Update the prompt, knowledge or policy
Best for
Simple routing
Narrow FAQs
End-to-end resolution of real calls
A voice bot is usually a narrower tool: it recognizes a set of phrases and replies from a script. An AI voice agent is what you get when that bot can reason, remember context across the call and use tools. In practice, many Indian enterprises run all three for now: IVR for routing, AI voice agents for high-volume journeys, and human agents for the calls that need judgment.
### How does an AI voice agent work?
An AI voice agent works in a loop that repeats for every turn of the call. Speech recognition turns the caller's words into text, a language model decides what they want and what to do, the agent calls APIs to act, and text to speech replies, all while it keeps listening for interruptions. Here is what happens at each step.
#### 1. Listening (speech recognition)
Automatic speech recognition (ASR)
turns the caller's audio into text as they speak. It also has to work out when they have finished, which is called endpointing. Cut in too early and you talk over people. Wait too long and the line goes awkwardly quiet.
#### 2. Understanding and deciding (language model)
The transcript goes to a
large language model (LLM)
, along with the call's goal, your business rules and whatever it knows about the caller. The model works out the intent ("wants to pay part of the EMI"), pulls out the details (₹2,500, today), and decides what to do next.
#### 3. Acting (tools and integrations)
If the next step needs data or an action, the agent
calls an API
: fetch the outstanding amount, create a payment link, update the CRM disposition, book a callback. That is where it becomes useful to the business and not just good at talking.
#### 4. Speaking (text to speech)
Text to speech (TTS)
turns the reply into audio. A good TTS voice gets the tone right, says "₹1,25,000" as "ek lakh pachees hazaar" and not "one hundred twenty-five thousand", and sounds the same from the first turn to the last.
#### 5. Turn-taking
The agent keeps listening while it talks. If the caller says "nahi nahi, wait", it should stop, drop the rest of its sentence and respond to the interruption. This barge-in handling is a big part of why a call feels like a conversation and not a recording.
#### The latency budget
People are fast at taking turns. A
>study of ten languages published in PNAS
(Stivers et al., 2009) found that the typical gap between one person finishing and the next starting is around 200 milliseconds, and the pattern held across languages and cultures. Callers notice when an agent is much slower than that.
Here is roughly where the time goes in a cascaded (ASR, LLM, TTS) pipeline on a phone call:
Step
Typical range
Endpointing (deciding the caller has stopped)
200-500 ms
Final transcript from ASR
100-300 ms
LLM first token
200-600 ms
TTS first audio chunk
100-250 ms
Telephony network, both ways
Total time to first word
about 0.7-2 seconds
Ranges are indicative and vary by vendor, model size, region and carrier.
Two practical points follow from this. First, latency adds up across vendors, so an agent assembled from four different APIs in four different regions starts at a disadvantage. Second, always measure on a real phone call over a mobile network, not on a browser demo over office Wi-Fi. Some newer systems use speech-to-speech models that skip the text step to save time, though most enterprise deployments still use the cascaded design because it is easier to control and audit.
#### Where an AI voice agent runs
The same agent can answer and make calls on several channels:
Phone lines (PSTN and SIP):
Most Indian enterprise calls, inbound and outbound, still run here, which is why phone audio quality matters so much.
WhatsApp voice calls:
Customers call a business from the app they already use every day. See how
WhatsApp AI agents
work for banks, NBFCs and hospitality.
Apps and websites:
A "talk to us" button that opens a voice session inside your app, usually with clearer wideband audio.
### Why are Indian languages harder for AI voice agents?
Indian calls are harder because of how people talk on them, not just how many languages there are. Phone audio is narrowband, callers mix two languages in one sentence, and amounts, dates and names follow patterns global models rarely see. An agent that misses "dhai hazaar" or confuses "kal" (yesterday or tomorrow) gets the business outcome wrong.
This is where most global AI voice agents struggle, and where the gap in published guides is widest. India has 22 scheduled languages and, by the
>2011 Census
, 121 languages with at least 10,000 speakers each. But the number of languages is not really the hard part. The hard part is how people actually talk on a customer call.
#### Phone audio is thin
Most customer calls in India still go over traditional telephone networks, which carry narrowband audio sampled at 8 kHz. That is half or less of the detail a speech model gets from a laptop microphone. Add a two-wheeler in traffic, a TV in the background or a weak signal in a basement, and models trained mostly on clean, wideband audio make far more mistakes. Ask any vendor what share of their training data is real 8 kHz telephony, in your languages, and ask for
telephony benchmarks
, not just clean-audio scores.
#### People mix languages in the same sentence
A caller in Mumbai does not pick Hindi or English. They use both, sometimes in one breath. Tamil and English, Kannada and English, Bengali and Hindi, the same thing happens everywhere. Here is how one ordinary sentence can go wrong:
Stage
Transcript
What the caller said
"Haan, mera auto-debit fail ho gaya, account mein balance kam tha."
English-first ASR (illustrative)
"Hum mera auto debit fail ho gaya account mein balance come the."
What the agent needs
Intent: auto-debit failed. Reason: low balance. Next: offer a payment link or a new debit date.
One wrong word ("come" for "kam") is enough to flip the meaning.
Speech recognition built for code-mixed speech
keeps the English words in English, the Hindi words in Hindi, and the meaning intact.
#### Numbers, money and dates are spoken differently
Amounts, dates and times are where calls are won or lost, especially in BFSI, and Indian speech has patterns most global models never see:
Spoken
Means
Why it trips up generic systems
dhai hazaar
₹2,500
"Dhai" (2.5) is not a standard number word
pachees sau
Same amount said as "25 hundred"
sava lakh
₹1,25,000
"Sava" means a quarter more, and lakh is not used outside South Asia
dedh crore
₹1.5 crore (₹15,000,000)
Indian place values (lakh, crore)
saade teen baje
3:30
"Saade" means plus a half
kal
Yesterday
or
tomorrow
Only the verb tense tells you which
parso
Day before yesterday
day after tomorrow
Same problem, two days out
If an agent hears "kal pay kar diya" (paid yesterday) as "will pay tomorrow", it logs a promise to pay that was actually a payment, and the customer gets another reminder they do not deserve. Small errors like this are why accuracy on numbers and dates matters more than overall word accuracy in collections and banking.
#### Names and product terms
Indian names, town names, PIN codes and brand or product names come up all the time, and they are exactly the words a general model is least likely to know. A consumer brand's support line has to hear "Crompton geyser" correctly whether it is said in Marathi, Telugu or Hinglish. Features like
keyterm prompting
, which tell the speech model which words to expect, make a measurable difference here.
#### Tone and respect
Speaking well matters as much as hearing well. Hindi callers expect "aap", not "tum". A "ji" in the right place lowers the temperature of a tense collections call. The agent's voice needs to
sound local
, not like an English voice reading Hindi text, and it needs to be firm or warm depending on the moment.
### Where do Indian enterprises use AI voice agents?
Indian enterprises use AI voice agents most on calls that are frequent, follow a pattern and have a clear outcome. Banks and NBFCs lead with EMI reminders, early collections and lead qualification, followed by insurance renewals, KYC, retail delivery and service calls, healthcare appointments, candidate screening and tier-1 contact center support.

)

Scale is where the economics change. One Gnani AI customer quoted on our homepage called more than 360,000 customers, found 29,000 who were interested, and attributed ₹25 crore in revenue to the program. A human outbound team of a few dozen people would need months to make that many calls.
#### When to keep a human on the line
An AI voice agent should not try to handle everything. Disputes, complaints about agent behavior, bereavement or claims involving loss, and customers who sound distressed should go to a person, quickly, with a summary and
live guidance for the human agent
so nobody has to repeat themselves. A well-designed agent knows when to hand off, and that is part of what you should test.
### What rules must an AI voice agent follow in India?
An AI voice agent calling Indian customers follows the same rules as your human teams. The main ones are TRAI's 1600 number series for financial service calls, TRAI's commercial communication rules, RBI's 8 am to 7 pm window for recovery calls, and consent and data obligations under the DPDP Act and Rules.
Treat the table below as a starting checklist for your compliance team, not legal advice.
Rule
What it means for voice agents
TRAI 1600-series numbering
TRAI directed
entities regulated by RBI, SEBI and PFRDA to use the 1600 number series for service and transactional calls, with deadlines from 1 January 2026 (commercial banks) to 15 March 2026 (qualified stockbrokers).
Insurers regulated by IRDAI
had to move by 15 February 2026. Outbound AI calls need to go out from the right series.
TRAI commercial communication rules (TCCCPR)
Promotional calls have to respect customer preferences and registered headers. Keep promotional and service calls clearly separate.
RBI conduct rules on recovery
Recovery calls cannot be made before 8 am or after 7 pm, and borrowers cannot be threatened or harassed.
RBI's updated directions
, effective 1 January 2027, also require recovery calls to be recorded with prior intimation to the borrower. Calling windows, scripts and recording must enforce this.
DPDP Act 2023 and DPDP Rules 2025
The
DPDP Rules were notified in November 2025
, with obligations phased in until May 2027. Plan for consent, purpose limits, notices, retention and breach handling on call recordings and transcripts.
Sector regulators (RBI, IRDAI)
Outsourcing, recording and data localization expectations differ by sector. Check where audio, transcripts and model processing physically live, or consider
sovereign AI
deployments.
Two practical takeaways. Put guardrails in code, not just in the prompt: calling-hour windows, banned phrases and mandatory disclosures should be enforced by the platform. And keep every call
recorded, transcribed, scored and searchable
, because when an auditor or a customer asks what was said, "the AI said it" is not an answer.
### How to evaluate an AI voice agent before you buy
To evaluate an AI voice agent, test it on your own recorded calls and on live mobile calls, not on a vendor demo. Check accuracy on amounts, dates and names, measure response time on slow calls, try to break it with interruptions and language switches, and confirm the right actions land in your systems.
Demos are always good. Your own calls tell you more. Here is a test plan that takes a week and saves months.
1. Test on your own audio:
Pull 200 to 300 real recorded calls across your top languages, including noisy ones, and run them through each vendor's speech recognition. Check accuracy on amounts, dates, names and product terms separately from overall word accuracy.
2. Make real phone calls:
Ring the agent from ordinary mobile phones, on different carriers, from a moving car and a busy market. Time the gap between when you stop talking and when it starts. Look at the slow calls (the 95th percentile), not just the average.
3. Try to break it:
Interrupt it mid-sentence. Switch from Tamil to English. Say "kal" and mean yesterday. Ask something off-script. Get angry. Ask for a human. Note what it does each time.
4. Check the actions, not just the words:
After each test call, look at your CRM or test system. Was the disposition right? Was the promise-to-pay date the date the caller actually said?
5. Ask how quality is checked at scale:
Nobody can listen to a million calls. Ask how the vendor
tests new versions before release
, how every live call is scored, and how you will
spot problems such as a rise in a particular complaint
6. Ask where everything runs:
Find out which models the vendor owns and which it rents from third parties, where audio and transcripts are stored, and whether you can deploy
in-region
, in a private cloud or on-premise if your regulator or security team requires it.
7. Price the whole call:
Per-minute rates leave out telephony, retries and the human time spent cleaning up after bad calls. Compare cost per resolved call.
Comparing specific platforms? See our
comparisons and alternatives
### How much does an AI voice agent cost?
AI voice agents are usually priced per minute of conversation, sometimes with a platform fee, and the final cost depends on call volume, languages, integrations and where the system is deployed. The rate card matters less than the cost of each call that actually gets resolved.
When you compare quotes, check what sits inside and outside the per-minute price:
Cost line
What to ask
Conversation minutes
Does the rate include speech recognition, the language model and text to speech, or are they billed separately?
Telephony
Are carrier minutes, numbers (including 1600-series) and SIP trunks included?
Retries and no-answers
Are unanswered and very short calls billed?
Setup and integrations
Is connecting your CRM, LOS or payment gateway a one-time fee or included?
Deployment
Does private cloud or on-premise deployment change the price?
Quality and monitoring
Are call recordings, transcripts, scoring and testing included?
A simple way to compare: take the total monthly cost and divide it by the number of calls that reached the right outcome (paid, renewed, verified, resolved). That figure tells you more than any per-minute rate.
### How Gnani AI builds AI voice agents for India
Gnani AI has been building speech technology for Indian languages for years, and that is still where the platform starts. We train and run our own models across the voice agent stack instead of stitching together third-party APIs:
Prisma v3.0
for speech recognition, including modes for code-mixed speech and keyterm prompting for names and product terms.
Timbre v3.0
for text to speech, with expressive voices and audio tags for tone.
Evon v3.3
, a language model calibrated for BFSI, insurance, healthcare and telecom conversations.
Agent API
to build and run voice AI agents from your own platform, and the Prompt Engine for scenario-based conversations.
Agentic Evals
for testing agents before release, and
AI Insights
for understanding what customers say across every live call.
The platform supports 40+ languages and is trained on more than 14 million hours of voice data. It runs in cloud, private cloud, on-premise and air-gapped setups, with in-region deployments in the US, Singapore, Japan and the UAE. More than 250 enterprises use it for collections, customer service, KYC, HR and sales calls.
### Start with the calls you already have
The best way to judge an AI voice agent is on your own calls, not a polished demo. Pick one high-volume journey, pull a few hundred real recordings, and see how each platform handles your languages, your numbers and your customers' interruptions.
Book a demo
with Gnani AI and bring those recordings. We will show you how our voice agents handle them in your languages, on real phone audio, with your rules built in.
### Frequently asked questions
What is an AI voice agent in simple terms?
An AI voice agent is a computer program that talks to people on the phone or in an app, understands what they say in normal language, and gets things done, such as booking, verifying, reminding or resolving a query. It works around the clock and can handle many calls at once.
What is the difference between a voice bot and an AI voice agent?
A voice bot usually follows a fixed script and recognizes a limited set of phrases. An AI voice agent uses a large language model to understand open speech, remember context through the call, handle interruptions and take actions in business systems. Most new deployments are AI voice agents.
Can an AI voice agent speak Hindi and other Indian languages?
Yes, but quality varies a lot. Look for speech recognition trained on Indian telephone audio, support for code-mixed speech such as Hinglish, correct handling of Indian number words like "dhai hazaar" and "sava lakh", and voices that sound native, not translated.
Are AI calling agents legal in India?
Yes, when they follow the same rules as human callers. Key requirements include TRAI's 1600 number series for regulated financial entities' service calls, TRAI's commercial communication rules, RBI's 8 am to 7 pm window for recovery calls, and consent and data obligations under the DPDP Act and Rules.
How fast should an AI voice agent respond?
Aim for the first word within about a second of the caller finishing, measured on real mobile calls. Human conversation runs on gaps of roughly 200 milliseconds, so delays much longer than a second feel unnatural and make callers talk over the agent.
Will AI voice agents replace human call center agents?
They take over high-volume, repetitive calls such as reminders, confirmations and first-level queries. Disputes, complaints, sensitive situations and complex sales still need people. Most enterprises use AI voice agents to let their human teams focus on those calls.
Can an AI voice agent make outbound calls?
Yes. AI voice agents handle both inbound calls, such as support and enquiries, and outbound calls, such as reminders, renewals, lead follow-ups and surveys. Outbound calling in India must follow TRAI numbering and consent rules, and RBI calling hours for recovery.
Should we build our own AI voice agent or buy a platform?
Building with open-source frameworks and third-party APIs gives you control, but you take on latency tuning, Indian-language accuracy, telephony, compliance and round-the-clock monitoring yourself. Most enterprises buy a platform for these and focus their own teams on journeys, integrations and business rules.

If your enterprise voice bot can’t be interrupted, it can’t be considered conversational. In the age of
autonomous AI agents
, barge-in is the silent enabler of human-like responsiveness — the one feature that transforms a scripted IVR into an intelligent, reactive, and emotionally aware interface. Yet, it remains one of the least discussed capabilities in the voice AI stack. This in-depth guide will walk you through:
The
history
and evolution of barge-in from legacy IVR systems to today’s AI-powered platforms
Why it’s
mission-critical
for enterprise voice bots
How barge-in works — from real-time audio streaming to interrupt-aware dialog management
Where it
delivers the most ROI
in high-value use cases like collections, onboarding, and support
Why most systems still fail at it — and how Gnani.ai solves it natively
Let’s dive in.
### The Genesis: Where Did Barge-In Come From?
Barge-in first emerged in the late 1980s as a technical enhancement in
telephony-based IVR systems
. Back then, IVRs were basic call-routing mechanisms, offering pre-recorded menu options that users had to listen to entirely before responding with a keypad input (DTMF). As these systems became more sophisticated and began accepting
voice input
, barge-in was introduced as a response to a growing problem —
user impatience
. Instead of waiting through a five-option prompt (“Press 1 for account balance...”), callers wanted to speak up the moment they recognized their intent. Barge-in was engineered to allow
mid-prompt interruption
, giving users control over the pace of the conversation.
#### Milestones in Barge-In Evolution:
1980s–90s
: Bell Labs, Dialogic, and Nortel experiment with barge-in for telephony IVRs
1996
: AT&T integrates barge-in for operator assist systems
2000s
: Speech-enabled IVRs adopt barge-in using basic keyword detection
2010s
: With the rise of mobile voice assistants, barge-in becomes a UX expectation
2020s
: AI-powered bots use NLP and streaming ASR to understand and redirect barge-in inputs in real time
What started as a telephony hack has evolved into a cornerstone of conversational AI architecture.
### What Is Barge-In Today — And Why Is It Crucial?
It is the system’s ability to
accept and respond to user input while a prompt is being delivered
. Unlike a call-and-response model, where the bot talks and then listens, barge-in-enabled bots can
talk and listen simultaneously
— a capability that makes conversations feel fluid and natural. In technical terms, barge-in is a composite of:
Full-duplex audio streaming
Voice activity detection (VAD)
Interrupt-aware dialogue orchestration
Low-latency ASR (Automatic Speech Recognition)
Intent override logic via NLP
It mimics how humans converse — overlapping, interrupting, and dynamically adjusting. And in today’s
voice-first enterprise
landscape
, this is not optional. It’s fundamental.
Without barge-in:
Users are forced into rigid conversation flows
Prompts can become long, repetitive, and irrelevant
Frustrated users hang up, abandon, or opt for human agents
CSAT drops and operational costs increase due to unnecessary escalations
#### With barge-in:
Conversations adapt in real time
Customers feel heard and in control
Faster resolutions drive lower AHT
Engagement rates and customer trust increase
### How It Works: Inside the Real-Time Tech Stack
Implementing barge-in is
technically non-trivial
. It requires a tightly orchestrated architecture capable of
streaming audio, detecting intent, and changing course in milliseconds
. Here’s what’s happening under the hood when a user interrupts a bot:
Full-Duplex Audio Streaming
Traditional bots operate in
half-duplex
mode: either speaking or listening. It needs
full-duplex
capability — the ability to
send and receive audio streams concurrently
. This requires optimized
audio pipelines
, real-time encoding, and stream handlers to ensure no overlap, distortion, or dropouts.
Voice Activity Detection (VAD)
VAD continuously monitors the input channel to distinguish between silence, noise, and speech. It uses acoustic models trained on varied environments — offices, streets, homes — to filter irrelevant sounds and recognize valid speech.
Low-Latency ASR Pipeline
As soon as speech is detected, ASR kicks in. For barge-in to feel human, ASR latency must be
sub-500ms
— with decoding starting
before
the user finishes speaking. Gnani.ai’s proprietary ASR is optimized for:
40+ Indian and global languages
Low-resource and noisy audio
Code-switched inputs (e.g., Hinglish, Tamlish)
Interrupt-Aware Dialogue Management
Once speech is decoded, the system checks if the user intent diverges from the current flow. If yes, it
cancels the active prompt mid-sentence
, pauses any streaming output, and redirects to a more relevant response node. This requires
session memory, context recovery, and fallback planning
— or else the system will either crash or restart, which is disastrous for CX.
Prompt Cancellation and Graceful Transition
A bot must
know how to stop speaking
— even mid-word — without sounding unnatural. At Gnani, we use
token-level interruption models
to end sentences cleanly and generate follow-ups that preserve flow and coherence.
### Use Cases
Let’s explore where barge-in is not just a feature, but a
mission-critical capability
.
Collections and Loan Reminders
Borrowers often interrupt with “Already paid,” “Send payment link,” or “Will pay next week.” A bot that continues reading the full reminder script causes irritation and leads to drop-offs. With barge-in:
Resolution time drops
Agents only handle escalations
### Frequently Asked Questions
What is barge-in in an IVR or voice bot?
Barge-in lets a voice bot accept and respond to user input while a prompt is still playing. Instead of forcing callers to sit through a full menu, the system talks and listens at the same time, which makes the conversation feel natural.
How does barge-in technology actually work?
It combines five layers: full duplex audio streaming, voice activity detection that separates speech from noise, speech recognition under 500 milliseconds of latency, interrupt aware dialogue management with session memory, and token level prompt cancellation so the bot stops speaking smoothly.
When did barge-in first appear in telephony?
Barge-in emerged in telephony IVRs during the 1980s and 1990s to address caller impatience with mandatory menu prompts. AT&T integrated it for operator assist in 1996. It spread through speech enabled IVRs in the 2000s and now runs on streaming recognition and NLP.
Why does barge-in reduce average handle time?
Because callers can say what they want immediately, rather than waiting for prompts to finish playing. Faster resolution lowers average handle time, cuts abandonment and reduces escalations to human agents. Barge in also supports higher engagement, better satisfaction scores and greater trust.
Can barge-in handle mixed languages like Hinglish?
Yes. Gnani.ai's speech recognition is optimised for over 40 Indian and global languages and handles code switched input such as Hinglish and Tamlish. On collections calls, for example, a borrower can interrupt with payment status and get an immediate, relevant response.

### TL;DR
Conversational AI is a set of technologies that lets software hold a two-way conversation with a person in natural language, over voice or text. It combines speech recognition, a reasoning model, speech synthesis and an orchestration layer that connects the conversation to business systems. A rule-based chatbot follows a fixed decision tree and fails when a caller phrases something unexpectedly. A conversational AI system infers intent from the words it actually hears, keeps context across turns, and completes the task. In enterprise contact centres it handles collections calls, appointment booking, onboarding, KYC and support, in the caller's own language.
### What is conversational AI?
Conversational AI describes software that understands what a person says or types, works out what they want, and responds in a way that moves the task forward. The phrase covers voice agents on a phone line, assistants inside a banking app, and agents that run on WhatsApp or SMS.
Two capabilities separate it from older automation. The first is intent recognition. The system maps a wide range of phrasings to the same underlying request, so "what's left on my card", "card balance please" and "kitna bacha hai" all resolve to a balance enquiry. The second is context. The system remembers what was said three turns ago, so a caller can say "and the other one" without repeating the account number.
Enterprise deployments add a third requirement that consumer assistants rarely face. The conversation has to complete a transaction inside a core system, under an audit trail, and hand off cleanly to a human when it cannot. That is the part that decides whether a deployment pays for itself.
### Conversational AI vs rule-based chatbots
The two get used interchangeably, and the difference matters when you are sizing a contact centre deployment. A rule-based bot is deterministic and cheap to build. It works well for a short, stable flow with few variations, such as an OTP confirmation. It breaks the moment a caller goes off script.
Conversational AI costs more to build and needs real training data, but it absorbs variation. The table below sets out where each one fits.
Conversational AI compared with rule-based chatbots
Dimension
Rule-based chatbot
Conversational AI
How it understands input
Keyword and pattern matching against a fixed script
Intent inferred from open language, including unseen phrasings
Memory across turns
None, or a single stored variable
Full conversation context carried through the session
Off-script caller
Falls through to a human or repeats the prompt
Reframes the question and continues
Language coverage
One script per language, written by hand
Multilingual at model level, including code-switched speech
Build effort
Low, but grows with every new branch
Higher upfront, and absorbs variation without new branches
Where it fits
Short, stable confirmations such as an OTP or a delivery slot
Collections, onboarding, KYC, support and any branching task
Main failure mode
Containment collapses as caller phrasing varies
Needs real training data and honest latency budgeting
Most enterprises end up running both. A rule-based flow handles the narrow, high-volume confirmations, and a conversational agent handles everything with branching or ambiguity.
ENTERPRISE VOICE AI
See Gnani AI's Voice AI Agent in action
200+ Enterprises · 30M daily calls · 10 Indic languages
Book A Demo
### The four layers of a conversational AI stack
Buyers often evaluate conversational AI as one product. It is cheaper to evaluate it as four layers, because each one fails differently and each one has its own latency budget.
#### Speech recognition
Speech to text turns audio into words. Accuracy here sets the ceiling for everything downstream, and telephony is the hard case: 8kHz audio, background noise, and callers who mix two languages in one sentence. Gnani AI trains
Prisma v2.5
on 14M+ hours of real telephonic audio, and reports under 4% word error rate on Indian speech, 96% code-switching accuracy, and sub-200ms streaming latency.
#### Reasoning
The reasoning layer decides what the caller wants and what to do about it. General-purpose models handle open conversation well but can be loose with policy and with numbers. Models tuned on domain language do better on the terms that matter in BFSI and insurance. Gnani AI's hosted reasoning model, Evon v2.0, covers 11+ Indic languages and is tuned for BFSI, insurance, healthcare and telecom, and the open-weight
Evon v3.3
ships 30B total parameters with roughly 3.5B active per token under Apache 2.0.
#### Speech synthesis
Text to speech returns the answer as audio. On a phone line the test is not studio fidelity, it is whether the voice stays natural at 8kHz and handles Indian names, lakh and crore cadence and code-switched sentences. Gnani AI reports MOS 4.23 on 8kHz telephony for
Timbre v2.5
, currently in Beta, with sub-100ms time to first audio across 10+ Indic languages.
#### Orchestration
Orchestration connects the conversation to CRM, core banking, ticketing and payment systems, fires the right agent on the right trigger, and writes the audit trail. Without it, a conversational agent answers questions but cannot finish a job. Gnani AI's orchestration layer,
Plexus
, is currently early access and waitlist only.
### Where conversational AI earns its keep
The deployments that pay back fastest share a pattern: high call volume, a repeatable task, and a clear system of record to write to.
Collections and recovery.
Outbound reminders, promise-to-pay capture, and settlement conversations at a volume no human team can cover. See
voice AI for debt collections
for how the workflow is structured.
Onboarding and KYC.
Document guidance, status chasing and verification steps that otherwise sit in a queue.
Customer support.
Balance, status and policy questions that make up the bulk of inbound volume. Gnani AI reports 80% of issues resolved on the first call across its
enterprise voice agents
.
Agent assist.
Rather than replacing the human, the system retrieves policy mid-call and writes the summary afterwards. Gnani AI reports a 90%+ reduction in after-call admin for
real-time agent assist
Quality and compliance monitoring.
Scoring every interaction instead of a 2% sample, and flagging breaches as they happen through
conversation analytics and QA
### What to test before you buy
Vendor demos run on clean audio and cooperative callers. Production does not. Four tests separate the systems that survive contact.
Your own call recordings.
Send a sample of real, de-identified calls from your worst line, not the vendor's sample set. Word error rate on clean 16kHz studio audio tells you nothing about an 8kHz mobile call from a noisy street.
Code-switched speech.
If your callers mix English with Hindi, Tamil or Bengali, test exactly that. Many systems that score well on monolingual benchmarks fall apart on Hinglish.
End-to-end latency, not component latency.
Measure from the caller finishing a sentence to the first audio coming back. Gnani AI reports under 800ms response latency in live conversations, and that is the number to compare against, not an isolated model figure.
Handoff quality.
Make the agent fail deliberately and watch what reaches the human. A transfer that drops the conversation history costs more than it saves.
When you compare vendor numbers, check that both sides measured the same thing. Time to first audio and p95 first byte are different metrics, and so is word error rate on telephony versus studio audio. Numbers measured differently do not compare directly.
### Deployment and compliance
Conversational AI in a regulated industry is a data-residency question as much as a model question. Gnani AI runs across cloud, private cloud, on-premise and air-gapped environments, and the
Artha sovereign stack
puts the full model stack inside infrastructure the customer controls.
Indian deployments fall under the DPDP Act. BFSI adds RBI guidance, insurance adds IRDAI, and outbound calling adds TRAI rules on consent and DND. US healthcare brings HIPAA, and EU data brings GDPR. Gnani AI is SOC 2 Type 2 certified and ISO 27001 certified, and HIPAA, GDPR and PCI-DSS compliant.
Call recordings, transcripts and call metadata are personal data, and voiceprints are sensitive biometric data. Treat retention and access as design decisions, not afterthoughts. Confirm with your legal and compliance team before deployment.
One more rule applies everywhere: a voice agent discloses that it is AI, in the opening line of the script. Build it into the prompt rather than bolting it on later.
### Where to start
If you are still deciding what is conversational AI worth to your contact centre, start by picking one high-volume, low-variation task and measuring it honestly: containment rate, average handle time, and the cost per contained interaction. Run the vendor against your own recordings in your own languages. Compare the shortlist on the
voice AI comparison hub
, and read through the rest of the
Gnani AI blog
for use-case detail by industry.
### Frequently asked questions
What is conversational AI in simple terms?
Conversational AI is software that holds a natural back-and-forth conversation with a person, by voice or text, and completes a task at the end of it. It listens, works out what the person wants, acts on it in a business system, and replies in the same language the person used.
What is the difference between conversational AI and a chatbot?
A chatbot usually follows a fixed decision tree and only recognises phrasings it was explicitly given. Conversational AI infers intent from open language and keeps context across turns, so it handles callers who go off script. The practical difference shows up in containment rate: rule-based flows drop the caller to a human as soon as the script runs out.
Does conversational AI work in Indian languages?
Yes, though quality varies sharply by vendor and by language. The constraint is training data: models trained mostly on English studio audio degrade on 8kHz Indian telephony. Gnani AI runs 10+ Indic languages in production speech recognition and reports 96% code-switching accuracy on mixed Hindi-English speech.
How long does a conversational AI deployment take?
A narrow use case on a single channel can be live in weeks rather than quarters, and Gnani AI reports under 20 minutes to go live for a basic agent. The schedule is usually set by integration and compliance review rather than by the model, so scope the core system connections early.
Is conversational AI safe for regulated industries?
It can be, provided the deployment model matches the regulation. On-premise and air-gapped options keep conversation data inside the customer network, which is how most RBI and IRDAI reviews get satisfied. Certifications tell you about the vendor's controls, not about your configuration, so confirm with your legal and compliance team before deployment.
What does conversational AI cost?
Gnani AI does not publish pricing, which is a disadvantage if you are trying to size a project quickly, and the same is true of most enterprise voice vendors. Developers can test the speech models directly through the API documentation before talking to anyone.

### Understanding Intent Recognition: The Foundation of Intelligent Interactions
Intent recognition
is the sophisticated process by which AI systems decode the true purpose behind user communications. Whether someone types a message, speaks into a microphone, or submits a form, intent recognition goes far beyond simple keyword matching to understand the underlying goal driving that interaction.
Think of it as digital mind-reading but powered by advanced algorithms rather than intuition.
#### The Mechanics Behind the Magic
Modern intent recognition systems employ a multi-layered approach:
Large Language Models (LLM)
form the foundation, breaking down human language into components that machines can understand. This includes parsing sentence structure, identifying key phrases, and recognizing context clues that reveal meaning.
Machine learning algorithms
then classify these parsed inputs into predefined categories or intents. For instance, "I can't access my dashboard" might be classified under "technical support," while "What's included in the premium plan?" falls under "product inquiry."
Entity extraction
identifies specific details within the communication—dates, account numbers, product names, or service tiers—that provide actionable context for the recognized intent.
Finally,
contextual understanding
considers the broader conversation history, user profile, and situational factors to refine the interpretation and ensure accuracy.
### Why Intent Recognition Matters More Than Ever in B2B SaaS
The B2B SaaS landscape has evolved dramatically over the past decade. Customer expectations have shifted from patience with slow, manual processes to demands for instant, accurate responses. This evolution makes intent recognition not just useful, but essential.

When customers reach out to your platform, they're often under pressure to solve problems quickly. Intent recognition enables immediate understanding of their needs, routing them to the right resources or providing instant solutions. Companies using intent recognition can dramatically reduce response times while achieving higher satisfaction scores and reduced churn rates.

Beyond customer-facing interactions, intent recognition powers sophisticated workflow automation. When a sales prospect submits a demo request, the system can instantly recognize this intent and trigger a series of automated actions: scheduling follow-ups, preparing personalized materials, and notifying the appropriate sales team members.

For B2B SaaS companies managing thousands of customer interactions daily, intent recognition becomes a force multiplier. Organizations report significantly reducing manual support workload while achieving high accuracy in query routing. It reduces the burden on support teams, ensures consistent service quality, and provides valuable insights into customer behavior patterns and emerging needs. Companies implementing comprehensive intent recognition see substantial cost savings through improved operational efficiency.

speech recognition capabilities

large language model understanding engine

authentication protocols

#### Real-Time Integration Excellence

secure API integrations

machine learning optimization

### Real-World Impact: Intent Recognition in Action
Consider a typical scenario in the financial services sector. A client calls with concerns about recent account activity, saying, "I noticed some unusual transactions on my business account last week, and I want to make sure everything is legitimate."

### What Is Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)?
Artificial intelligence has moved fast. But enterprise adoption has moved cautiously. The reason is not lack of ambition. The reason is trust, accuracy, and control. This is exactly where
retrieval augmented generation
becomes critical.
Large language models are powerful. They can write, summarize, reason, and converse. But by themselves, they operate in isolation from your business data. They do not know your policies, your documentation, your customer history, or your internal knowledge base. This gap is where hallucinations happen. This gap is where enterprise AI breaks.
Retrieval augmented generation
is the architectural breakthrough that closes this gap.
In this blog, we will break down what retrieval augmented generation is, why it matters, how it works, where it is used, and why it has become the default foundation for enterprise-grade generative AI systems.
### Understanding the Core Problem with Traditional LLMs
Before understanding retrieval augmented generation, it is important to understand the limitation it solves.
Traditional large language models are trained on massive public and licensed datasets. Once training is complete, the model’s knowledge is frozen. It cannot natively access your databases, internal documents, product manuals, CRM systems, or policy repositories.
This leads to four major enterprise risks:
Responses that sound confident but are factually incorrect
Outdated information with no real-time context
No grounding in proprietary or regulated data
Limited explainability and traceability
For consumer use cases, this may be acceptable. For BFSI, healthcare, telecom, government, or SaaS platforms, this is unacceptable.
This is exactly why
was introduced.
### What Is Retrieval Augmented Generation?
is a generative AI architecture that combines two systems working together.
The first system retrieves relevant information from an external knowledge source.
The second system uses a language model to generate a response grounded in that retrieved information.
In simple terms, retrieval augmented generation allows an AI model to “look up” facts before answering.
Instead of relying only on what the model learned during training, retrieval augmented generation injects real, contextual, enterprise-approved data into the prompt at runtime.
This makes responses more accurate, auditable, and business-aligned.
### Why Retrieval Augmented Generation Matters for Enterprises
Retrieval augmented generation is not a feature. It is an architectural necessity.
Enterprises operate on dynamic data. Policies change. Product catalogs evolve. Regulations update. Customer interactions are contextual.
Without retrieval augmented generation, generative AI becomes risky at scale.
With retrieval augmented generation, AI becomes:
• Grounded in factual data
• Aligned with enterprise knowledge
• Safer for regulated industries
• Easier to govern and audit
• Faster to deploy without retraining models
This is why most serious enterprise AI platforms today are built around retrieval augmented generation by default.
### How Retrieval Augmented Generation Works Step by Step
To understand retrieval augmented generation clearly, let us break it down into a practical flow.
#### Step 1: Data Ingestion and Indexing
Enterprise data is first ingested from sources such as PDFs, documents, databases, CRM systems, FAQs, call transcripts, or knowledge bases.
This data is then chunked and converted into vector embeddings using an embedding model.
These embeddings are stored in a vector database.
This step ensures your internal knowledge is searchable in semantic form.
#### Step 2: Query Understanding
When a user asks a question, the query is converted into an embedding.
This embedding represents the intent and meaning of the question.
#### Step 3: Retrieval
The system searches the vector database for the most relevant chunks of information based on semantic similarity.
Only the top, most relevant results are selected.
This retrieval step is the heart of retrieval augmented generation.
#### Step 4: Augmented Prompt Creation
The retrieved content is injected into the prompt along with the user query.
The language model is instructed to answer using only the provided context.
This ensures the output stays grounded in enterprise data.
#### Step 5: Generation
The language model generates a response using the retrieved information.
The result is a contextual, accurate, and enterprise-safe answer.
This entire pipeline is what defines
.
### Retrieval Augmented Generation vs Fine-Tuning
A common question enterprises ask is whether retrieval augmented generation replaces fine-tuning.
The answer is simple. They solve different problems.
Fine-tuning teaches a model how to behave.
Retrieval augmented generation teaches a model what to know.
Fine-tuning is expensive, slow, and static.
Retrieval augmented generation is dynamic, scalable, and cost-efficient.
For most enterprise use cases, retrieval augmented generation delivers faster ROI with lower risk.
This is why retrieval augmented generation is preferred for customer support, compliance, analytics, and operational workflows.
### Key Benefits of Retrieval Augmented Generation
Retrieval augmented generation delivers measurable business value.
#### Accuracy and Reduced Hallucinations
By grounding responses in retrieved data, retrieval augmented generation significantly reduces hallucinations.
The model no longer guesses. It responds based on facts.
#### Real-Time Knowledge Updates
Because retrieval augmented generation pulls data at runtime, updates reflect immediately.
No retraining required.
#### Enterprise Data Security
Data remains within enterprise systems.
Only relevant snippets are passed to the model.
This aligns with security and compliance requirements.
#### Explainability and Auditability
Responses can be traced back to source documents.
This is critical for regulated industries.
#### Faster Deployment Cycles
Retrieval augmented generation allows enterprises to deploy AI systems in weeks, not months.
### Common Use Cases of Retrieval Augmented Generation
Retrieval augmented generation is already powering real-world enterprise systems.
#### Customer Support and Contact Centers
AI agents use retrieval augmented generation to answer customer queries based on internal knowledge bases, policy documents, and historical tickets.
This improves first-contact resolution and reduces agent dependency.
#### Sales Enablement
Sales teams use retrieval augmented generation to query product documentation, pricing, competitive intelligence, and proposals in real time.
#### Compliance and Risk Management
Retrieval augmented generation enables AI systems to answer compliance queries using approved regulatory documents and internal SOPs.
#### Enterprise Search
Internal teams use retrieval augmented generation as a conversational interface over enterprise data silos.
#### Analytics and Insights
AI systems retrieve structured and unstructured data, then generate insights using retrieval augmented generation.
### Architecture Considerations for Retrieval Augmented Generation
Building retrieval augmented generation systems requires thoughtful design.
Key components include:
• High-quality data ingestion pipelines
• Efficient vector databases
• Robust chunking and metadata strategies
• Secure access controls
• Prompt orchestration and grounding rules
Poor implementation leads to poor retrieval.
Good retrieval leads to reliable generation.
Retrieval augmented generation is only as strong as the data strategy behind it.
### Challenges with Retrieval Augmented Generation
While powerful, retrieval augmented generation is not plug and play.
Common challenges include:
• Poor document chunking
• Low-quality embeddings
• Irrelevant retrieval results
• Prompt leakage
• Latency at scale
These challenges are solvable with the right architecture and operational discipline.
Enterprises that invest early in retrieval quality outperform those that treat it as an afterthought.
### The Future of Retrieval Augmented Generation
Retrieval augmented generation is evolving rapidly.
Future systems will include:
• Multi-modal retrieval across text, voice, images, and video
• Real-time streaming retrieval
• Memory-aware retrieval augmented generation
• Agentic workflows powered by retrieval augmented generation
• Deeper integration with enterprise APIs
As AI moves from chat to action, retrieval augmented generation will remain the backbone.
### Why Retrieval Augmented Generation Is the Default Enterprise Standard
The industry has moved past experimentation.
Enterprises now demand:
• Accuracy
• Control
• Governance
• ROI
Retrieval augmented generation delivers all four.
This is why retrieval augmented generation is no longer optional. It is foundational.
Any enterprise deploying generative AI without retrieval augmented generation is accepting unnecessary risk.
### Final Thoughts
Retrieval augmented generation is not just a technical concept. It is a strategic enabler.
It allows enterprises to scale AI safely, responsibly, and effectively.
It bridges the gap between generic intelligence and business-specific intelligence.
If you are serious about deploying generative AI in production, retrieval augmented generation is where you start.
If you are evaluating generative AI for your enterprise and want to implement
the right way, now is the time to act.
Talk to our AI experts to design a production-grade retrieval augmented generation architecture tailored to your data, workflows, and compliance needs.
Build AI systems that are accurate, reliable, and enterprise-ready.
Get started today.
Book a RAG Architecture Review
### Frequently Asked Questions
What is retrieval augmented generation, or RAG?
RAG combines an information retrieval system with a language model so the AI can look up facts before answering, rather than relying only on its training data. This reduces hallucination risk when a model needs current, enterprise specific information.
How does the RAG process work step by step?
Data is ingested, chunked, converted into vector embeddings, and stored. A query is turned into an embedding, a semantic search finds relevant content in the vector database, that content is injected into the prompt, and the model generates a grounded response.
What is the difference between RAG and fine-tuning?
Fine tuning teaches a model how to behave and requires retraining to update, while RAG teaches a model what to know by keeping data external. RAG is more dynamic, scalable, and cost efficient than fine tuning for changing information.
Where is RAG used in enterprises?
Named use cases include customer support powered by a knowledge base, sales enablement for pricing and competitive information, compliance and risk management grounded in regulatory documents, enterprise search, and analytics that synthesize structured and unstructured data.
What can go wrong with a RAG implementation?
RAG is only as strong as the data strategy behind it. Poor document chunking, low quality embeddings, irrelevant retrieval, prompt leakage, and latency at scale are common implementation challenges that can undermine an otherwise sound deployment.

There was a time when talking to a machine felt futuristic. Today, it’s expected. From barking commands at Alexa to navigating IVR hellholes, we’ve come a long way. But
Voice AI
— the kind that understands, acts, adapts, and sounds human — is a different beast entirely. This blog dives into how Voice AI started, who built it, how it evolved, where it’s used, how it impacts revenue, and what’s coming next.
### The Origins: From IVRs to Intelligent Speech
Voice interaction technology began in the
1950s
with Bell Labs'
Audrey system
, which could recognize digits spoken by a single voice. Progress was slow — in the 1980s and 90s, speech systems were limited to predefined commands or numeric menus. Companies like
IBM, Dragon Systems, AT&T
, and
Nuance
began commercializing speech-to-text systems. The goal wasn’t AI — it was automation: pressing 1 without pressing 1. These systems formed the foundation of
IVR (Interactive Voice Response)
, used heavily in telecom and banking. But they weren’t conversational. They were structured, robotic, and brittle.
### The First Wave of Voice Assistants
The 2000s changed that. Enter
Siri
(acquired by Apple in 2010),
Google Voice
, and later
Alexa
and
Cortana
. These voice assistants moved beyond touch-tone replacement. They could:
Understand questions
Respond conversationally
Offer information (weather, directions, reminders)
But they were still
command-based
. Their capabilities were narrow, and they didn’t understand
context, memory, or intent
deeply.
### The LLM Era: Voice Gets Smarter
The 2020s saw the rise of
LLMs (Large Language Models)
SLMs (Small Language Models)
. Suddenly, machines could:
Parse unstructured voice inputs
Understand multilingual code-mixed speech
Carry forward context across turns
Personalize conversations based on history
Trigger backend workflows in real time
Platforms like
Inya.ai
by
Gnani
took this further — combining real-time
multilingual ASR
, API execution, and memory into enterprise-grade voice bots.
### So What Exactly Is Voice AI?
Voice AI is not just ASR (speech-to-text). It’s a stack of technologies that enables machines to have human-like conversations over voice. It includes:
ASR (Automatic Speech Recognition)
– Converts voice to text
NLU (Natural Language Understanding)
– Understands meaning and intent
Dialog Management
– Chooses what to say/do next
TTS (Text-to-Speech)
– Speaks back to the user
LLM/SLM layer
– Adds reasoning, personality, memory
API orchestration
– Executes actions, not just replies
Together, this makes Voice AI
a fully interactive human-machine interface
.
### Who’s Using Voice AI — And Why?
Voice AI isn’t just a tech demo anymore. It’s running millions of conversations daily across industries:
Banking & Finance
EMI reminders, collections, fraud alerts
Loan pre-approvals, onboarding
Voice-based KYC
#### Telecom
Plan renewals, troubleshooting
Barring/unbarring flows
Automated DND registration

Appointment scheduling
Insurance verification
Post-consult follow-ups
#### Retail & Ecommerce
COD confirmation
Delivery updates
Feedback collection
#### Travel & Airlines
Booking confirmation
Rescheduling
Multilingual support for ticketing
#### Education
Exam reminders
Admissions support
Language tutoring bots
### How Does It Help? Revenue, Retention & Reach
Voice AI drives direct business impact:
✅
Faster resolution
= Lower AHT (Average Handling Time)
24/7 service
= No dependency on human hours
Multilingual reach
= Tap into new segments (tier 2–4 cities)
Higher conversions
= Voice-based upsell, lead re-engagement
Better recovery
= Automated reminders + real-time payme
### Frequently Asked Questions
What is voice AI?
Voice AI is technology that lets machines hold spoken conversations with people. It runs on a six part stack: speech recognition, natural language understanding, dialogue management, text to speech, a language model layer using large and small models, and API orchestration to complete actions.
How did voice AI develop over time?
It started in the 1950s with a Bell Labs system that recognised spoken digits from one speaker. Commercial speech to text followed, then IVR, which stayed rigid. The 2000s brought consumer voice assistants, still command based, and the 2020s brought language models that handle unstructured speech.
How does voice AI handle mixed language speech?
Language models let systems parse unstructured input, including code mixed speech where speakers switch languages mid sentence, while retaining context across the conversation. Inya.ai combines real time multilingual speech recognition, API execution and memory in one platform.
What does voice AI do in banking and telecom?
In banking it handles EMI reminders, collections, fraud alerts, loan pre approvals and voice based KYC. In telecom it covers plan renewals, troubleshooting and DND registration. Healthcare uses include appointment scheduling and insurance verification, while retail and travel use it for confirmations and updates.
What business benefits does voice AI deliver?
Benefits include lower average handling time, availability around the clock without depending on staffing, multilingual reach into tier two to tier four cities, and higher conversion and debt recovery. The gains come from automating conversations that previously needed a human agent.

An AI voice agent is software that holds a spoken conversation with a customer and completes the task they called about, without a human in the loop for the routine path. It is the layer most enterprises reach for after their IVR stops scaling. This guide covers what an AI voice agent actually is, the architecture underneath it, where deployments go wrong, and what a realistic rollout looks like in a regulated contact centre.
### TL;DR
An AI voice agent listens, understands intent, decides what to do, acts against back-office systems and speaks back, all inside a conversation. It differs from an IVR because the customer is not navigating a menu, and from a chatbot because speech introduces a hard latency budget: anything over roughly a second of silence reads as a dropped call. Enterprise deployments succeed or fail on four things rather than on model quality alone: integration depth into core systems, latency under load, language coverage that matches the actual caller base, and guardrails that produce an audit trail. In India the compliance surface includes the DPDP Act, RBI guidance for BFSI, IRDAI for insurance and TRAI rules for outbound calling.
### What an AI Voice Agent Is
#### The working definition
An AI voice agent is a system that converts speech to text, interprets intent and context, selects an action, executes that action against enterprise systems, and returns a spoken response, continuously, for the length of a call. The defining property is that it completes work. A system that only answers questions is an assistant. A system that updates a payment plan, books a slot or verifies a claim is an agent.
#### How it differs from an IVR and from a chatbot
An IVR asks the customer to map their problem onto a numbered menu designed by someone else. An AI voice agent lets the customer state the problem in their own words and in their own language. A text chatbot has no latency floor that the user can hear, so it can take a second to think. In voice, the same pause is interpreted as the line going dead, which is why speech systems are engineered to a response budget rather than to an accuracy target alone.
Dimension
Legacy IVR
Scripted voicebot
AI voice agent
How the caller navigates
Presses keys against a menu designed in advance.
Speaks, but only phrases the grammar was built for.
States the problem in their own words and own language.
Handles interruption
No. The prompt plays to the end.
Partially, through barge-in on fixed prompts.
Yes. The agent stops, re-plans and continues in context.
Completes a task
Routes the call. Work happens after transfer.
Captures a few fields, then transfers.
Executes against CRM, core banking or policy systems inside the call.
Code-switched speech
Not applicable.
Usually fails, because grammars are single-language.
Handled, when the recognition model was trained on code-mixed telephony audio.
Changing the flow
A release cycle in the IVR platform.
Rewriting and retesting the dialogue grammar.
Updating policy, prompts and tools, with the audit trail retained.
What it is good at
Deterministic routing at very low cost.
Short, highly repetitive transactions.
Open-ended conversations that end in a completed action.
Main failure mode
Caller abandons the menu and asks for an agent.
Caller falls outside the grammar and loops.
Integration gaps, so intent is captured but nothing is completed.
IVR, scripted voicebot and AI voice agent compared
### How an AI Voice Agent Works
#### The components
Speech recognition.
Converts caller audio to text. Telephony audio is 8kHz and noisy, so a model trained on studio recordings degrades badly here.
Prisma v2.5
is trained on more than 14 million hours of real telephonic audio and reaches under 4% word error rate on Indian speech, with 96% accuracy on code-switched Hinglish, Tanglish and Benglish.
Reasoning and dialogue control.
Decides what the caller wants and what to do next, holding state across turns and handling interruption.
Action layer.
Calls the CRM, core banking system, policy administration system or ticketing tool. This is the part that turns a conversation into a completed task.
Speech synthesis.
Returns the response as audio, with prosody that fits the context. Collections and support need different registers.
Guardrails and observability.
Policy checks, escalation rules, logging and audit. See the
Gnani AI model stack
for how the layers fit together.
#### The latency budget
Response latency is the single number that decides whether a call feels like a conversation. Gnani AI reports sub-200ms streaming latency for recognition in
and under 800ms end-to-end response latency in live conversations on
Gnani Agents
. A separate path removes the text hop entirely:
Gnani Warp v2.0
is a 5 billion parameter model that processes speech to speech directly, with no intermediate text layer, at sub-200ms P95.
#### Scale and guardrails
Peak load is where pilots break. Prisma v2.5 supports more than 35,000 simultaneous streams, which matters when a billing cycle or a campaign puts the whole book on the phone at once. On the governance side,
Gnani Plexus
, which is in early access on a waitlist, composes agents into workflows with guardrails, observability and audit logging built in rather than bolted on.
### Where Enterprises Deploy Them
#### Banking and collections
Early-bucket collections is the most common first deployment, because the conversation is bounded, the outcome is measurable and the volume justifies automation. The agent confirms identity, states the amount, negotiates within an approved band and records a promise to pay. See
voice AI for debt collections
and
agentic AI for banking
.
#### Insurance
Renewal reminders, claim status and first notice of loss are high-volume and heavily scripted today, which makes them a clean fit. IRDAI rules on disclosure and suitability shape what the agent may say.
#### BPO and contact centres
Deflecting repeat contact types frees human agents for the conversations that need judgment. Gnani AI reports 60% or greater reduction in operational costs and 80% of issues resolved on the first call across its deployments, with go-live inside 20 minutes for standard configurations. See
agentic AI for BPO and contact centres
### Why Deployments FailWhy Deployments Fail
Integration treated as phase two.
An agent that cannot write to the system of record only collects intent, which is a worse IVR. Build the action layer first.
Benchmarks run on clean audio.
Accuracy measured on 16kHz studio recordings does not predict accuracy on an 8kHz mobile call from a moving vehicle. Test on your own call recordings.
Handoff designed as a dead end.
When the agent escalates, the human needs the full conversation history. Without it the customer repeats themselves and the deflection saving is cancelled by the complaint.
Language coverage assumed rather than measured.
Pull the actual language distribution from your recordings before choosing which ones to launch. Code-switched speech is usually a larger share than anyone expects.
No observability until something breaks.
Latency, containment and escalation rates need instrumenting on day one, not after the first bad week.
### Compliance and Data Residency
Three things govern whether a deployment is allowed to run. First, the agent discloses that it is AI, stated in the opening lines of every script and prompt. Second, call recordings, transcripts and customer identifiers are personal data under the DPDP Act, and voiceprints and speaker embeddings count as sensitive biometric data with a higher bar again. Third, outbound calling in India sits under TRAI rules covering consent and DND registration.
Where the model runs is a design decision rather than a vendor constraint. Deployment spans cloud, private cloud, on-premise and air-gapped, and
Gnani Artha
packages the model stack for infrastructure the customer controls, so residency requirements are met by placement rather than by contract language. Gnani AI is SOC 2 Type 2 certified and ISO 27001 certified, and the platform is HIPAA, GDPR and PCI-DSS compliant. Confirm with your legal and compliance team before deployment.
### A Realistic Rollout Plan for an AI Voice Agent
Start with one intent, one language and one channel. Pick an intent with a clear completion event, so containment is measurable rather than inferred. Run the agent alongside the existing queue rather than in front of it, and route a fixed share of traffic to it so you have a live comparison.
Instrument four numbers from the first call: containment rate, escalation rate, end-to-end response latency at p95, and customer-reported satisfaction on handled calls. Widen by language before you widen by intent, because language coverage is where the recognition layer is tested hardest and where a weakness is cheapest to find early.
An AI voice agent earns its place when it completes work the queue used to absorb. The deployments that hold up are the ones where integration, latency and escalation were designed before the conversation script was written. To see the stack against your own call recordings,
book a demo
### Frequently asked questions
What is an AI voice agent?
An AI voice agent is software that holds a spoken conversation with a customer and completes the task they called about. It converts speech to text, interprets intent, acts against enterprise systems such as a CRM or core banking platform, and speaks the response back, without a human on the routine path.
How is an AI voice agent different from an IVR?
An IVR asks the caller to map their problem onto a numbered menu. An AI voice agent lets the caller state the problem in their own words and own language, handles interruption, and completes the task inside the call instead of routing it onward.
What latency does an AI voice agent need?
Voice has a hard response budget, because a pause longer than about a second reads as a dropped call. Gnani AI reports sub-200ms streaming recognition latency for Prisma v2.5 and under 800ms end-to-end response latency in live conversations on Gnani Agents.
Can an AI voice agent handle Hinglish and other code-switched speech?
Yes, when the recognition model was trained on code-mixed telephony audio rather than clean studio English. Gnani AI reports 96% code-switching accuracy for Prisma v2.5 across Hinglish, Tanglish and Benglish, from a corpus of more than 14 million hours of real telephonic audio.
Does an AI voice agent have to tell the customer it is AI?
Yes. Gnani AI requires every voice agent script and prompt to disclose that the customer is speaking with an AI agent, in the opening lines. Outbound calling in India also sits under TRAI rules on consent and DND registration. Confirm the exact wording with your legal and compliance team before deployment.
Why do enterprise AI voice agent deployments fail?
Most commonly because integration is treated as a later phase, so the agent captures intent but completes nothing; because accuracy was benchmarked on clean audio rather than 8kHz telephony; because escalation hands the customer to a human with no conversation history; or because language coverage was assumed rather than measured from actual call recordings.

Conversational AI—the future
